Arxiv abstract:
Most existing single image haze removal algorithms rely on a sufficient density of haze-free/low-haze image pairs to learn the transmission map for restoration. In this paper, we propose a fast single image haze removal algorithm that does not require any image pairs at all and is specifically designed to be fast in practice. The algorithm optimizes the haze visibility measure directly in the wavelet domain, resulting in a fast implementation. Furthermore, to overcome the drawback of the wavelet domain, i.e., non-differentiability, we propose a multilevel wavelet decomposition, where the optimization is performed at different levels of decomposition, yielding a successively differentiable algorithm. In addition, to further accelerate the optimization process, we propose an auxiliary function method that converges faster than simply using the non-differentiable wavelet domain haze visibility measure as the objective function. Our method is fast, with less than 0.1 seconds to remove haze on a single image, and can be readily used in any device, even on mobile devices.

Recent progress in the controlled generation of individual x-ray photons for imaging at a free-electron laser (XFEL) facility lays the foundation for a new regime of imaging – single-photon counting (SPC) imaging. In SPC imaging, the detected intensity at each image pixel is determined by counting the number of detected photons arriving within a fixed-length shutter time. In this paper, we investigate the benefits as well as the associated challenges of SPC imaging, as compared to conventional (i.e. integrating) imaging, in a variety of scientific applications. To this end, we have developed a simulation framework, which models the entire photon generation, propagation, and detection process at an XFEL facility, and which is suitable for performing fully-sequential simulations, wherein each detected photon's arrival time and pixel position is determined stochastically. In this paper we present the formalism and the numerical methods employed in this simulation framework. We then explore, through a series of numerical simulations, the relative benefits of SPC imaging as compared to conventional imaging in the context of three scientific applications: (a) phase imaging to recover a weak object transmission function; (b) diffraction imaging to determine an object's lattice; (c) imaging through strongly scattering media.

Abdominal CT images provide fine-grained details of the liver anatomy, which is widely used for clinical diagnosis and intervention. However, the complex anatomical structures in CT images make liver segmentation a challenging task, even for expert radiologists. In this paper, we present an auto-context neural network together with a self-supervised contour attention module to address the segmentation challenge. The auto-context module captures the global context by aggregating all positions and channels of the input features, while the self-supervised contour attention module is designed to capture the contour information of the objects, without any additional contour information in the training phase. We evaluate our method on the 2018 ISBI Liver Segmentation Challenge. Compared to the state-of-the-art methods, our approach produces segmentation results with better accuracy and spatial coherence, ultimately improving the F1-score from 87.1% to 89.4% on the challenge dataset.

Recent progress in deep learning has enabled the development of end-to-end trainable systems for self-driving. However, training such systems is challenging due to the lack of large-scale, diverse, and realistic training data. We introduce GeoSim, a video simulation system that generates geometrically-accurate, photorealistic training data for deep learning-based self-driving systems. GeoSim is designed to address the limitations of current simulation systems, which often produce unrealistic and synthetic-looking images. It uses a combination of geometric reasoning, physical simulation, and artistic rendering to generate realistic and diverse training data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GeoSim in generating realistic training data and show that it improves the performance of deep learning-based self-driving systems.

Semantic image segmentation, as a fundamental task in computer vision, aims at assigning semantic labels to each pixel in an image. Recently, deep learning methods have shown promising results in this area. However, most existing methods rely on greedy inference, which can result in suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic image segmentation based on Deep Gaussian CRFs (DGCRFs), which are a class of probabilistic models that leverage deep features learned by convolutional neural networks. By formulating the segmentation problem as a probabilistic inference problem, our approach is able to produce more accurate and robust predictions. We introduce a fast and exact inference algorithm that scales to realistic images.

Most existing works on clustering rely on distance functions to define a metric between data points, which assumes the data lies in a low-dimensional space and fails when the data lies on a manifold of higher dimension. In this paper, we propose a new clustering framework that does not rely on distance functions and hence is capable of clustering points on a manifold of any dimension. In particular, given a set of n points in d-dimensional space, our method first maps these n points to a kernel feature space, where kernel functions define a similarity metric between points. Next, we propose a spectral clustering algorithm that clusters points based on the similarity metric in the feature space. We show that the proposed method can be used to define a data-dependent metric between points, and hence can cluster points on a manifold of high dimension. We present experimental results on synthetic and real-world data sets, and show that the proposed method gives better clustering accuracy compared with state-of-the-art clustering methods.

We introduce a new estimator for the intrinsic dimension of a finite collection of data points, induced by the Gaussian core model. This model captures the local geometry around a data point through a truncated multivariate normal distribution. The intrinsic dimension is the dimension of the smallest space in which the data can be embedded in such a way that each data point has a neighborhood that is an analog of the model. We show that our estimator is consistently estimated, and suggest an iterative algorithm to compute it. This algorithm is validated against synthetic data, and the model is applied to several real world data sets. In particular, we show that on the "Ising" model, the intrinsic dimension grows as the dimension of the ambient space grows.

Abstract
 We present a deep learning work flow for fast and robust segmentation of anatomical structures in CT images. The network was trained on publicly available datasets with ground truth annotations for lung and spine. Our network is based on a convolutional neural network architecture previously validated on the MIAS challenge. We exploit existing clinically available delineations, which are used for treatment planning, for the initialization of the network. The initializations are propagated through the network using a weighted vector flow scheme.

We present the results of deep X-ray observations of two cometary blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies, Mrk 59 and Mrk 71, aimed at studying the nature of the excess soft X-ray emission recently discovered in these objects. The observations were performed with Chandra ACIS-S on 2005 November 22 (Mrk 59) and 2005 December 2 (Mrk 71) for a total exposure of ~70 ks and ~140 ks, respectively. The X-ray images of both galaxies are well fitted by a model in which the emission is dominated by a point source, most likely the active nucleus, at the galaxy's center, and a diffuse, unresolved component. The latter is spatially coincident with the optical emission and accounts for ~70% of the total X-ray flux in both galaxies. The spectrum of this diffuse component is well fitted by an absorbed power law with a photon index of ~1 and a cutoff at ~1 keV. The absorbed fluxes of the nuclei are ~2.5

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionise medical imaging, but also carries the risk of perpetuating and even increasing existing health inequalities. An international collaboration of experts from diverse fields has come together to consider how to ensure that AI in medical imaging is developed and deployed to maximise the benefits and minimise the harms. Following a two-stage online consultation, we used a modified Delphi method to achieve consensus on key issues, and we provide here a summary of our discussions and recommendations for future AI development and deployment. Combining the principles of trustworthy AI with consideration of fairness and equity, we propose a framework to inform the development and deployment of AI in medical imaging. To ensure the trustworthy and fair use of AI in medical imaging, developers, clinicians and researchers should consider the following: promoting health equality and equity; upholding data privacy and security; maintaining technical performance; supporting clinical performance and decision making; and being responsive to patients and the public. In this report, we outline a consensus view on the key issues that need to be addressed, and make recommendations for the future development and deployment of AI in medical imaging.

Post-mortem identification is an important task of forensic science, and the iris is a biologically unique region for human identification. However, the process of post-mortem iris image segmentation is extremely challenging due to the absence of ocular illumination and specularity. In this paper, we propose a deep learning based approach for post-mortem iris image segmentation, which is lightweight and efficient. Our approach is composed of a coarse segmentation network, which is a lightweight ResNet18 with an attention module, and a refined segmentation network, which is a U-Net with an attention module. We train our networks using a hybrid loss function, which combines dice loss and mse loss. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a public post-mortem iris image segmentation benchmark while being much faster than other approaches.

We present a comprehensive spectroscopic survey of stellar populations in the inner Galactic bulge, performed with the Fiber Multi-Object Spectrograph (FMOS) on the Subaru 8.2m telescope as a part of the Bulge Extinction Study (BES). The sample includes 555 stars with extinction-corrected magnesium abundances [Mg/H] < -1.7, covering a magnitude range of 12 < I < 17 mag. This survey largely complements the previous works, especially the recent study by Saito et al., who targeted the redder bulge stars with [Mg/H] < -2.3. Thanks to the large dataset, we can examine the stellar metallicity distribution in the inner bulge in detail, through construction of the MDF in several different ways. An apparent bimodality is seen in the MDF, which reflects the well-known division of the Galactic bulge into a metal-rich component and a metal-poor component.

Recent experiments on magneto-dielectric particle chains have revealed intriguing phenomena, including the observation of single-mode propagation in certain frequency ranges and the existence of frequency bands with no propagating modes. To explain these experimental observations, we have performed 3D full-wave simulations based on the transmission line model (TLM) and compared the results to those obtained from an effective continuum model. By comparing the results for different geometries, we found good agreement between our simulations and the experimental observations. The simulations show that the observed single-mode propagation is a result of the specific chain geometry and the choice of material properties. In addition, we found that the absence of propagating modes in certain frequency bands is a result of the interaction between the magnetic and dielectric responses of the particles. Our results suggest that the observation of single-mode propagation and the existence of frequency bands with no propagating modes can be explained by the specific chain geometry and the choice of material properties.

Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, with a goal to assign semantic labels to every pixel in an input image. Most existing works focus on designing complex models to learn direct mappings from images to segmentation labels, which limit their applicability in real-world applications due to the model's complexity and resource intensity. In this work, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation that utilizes psychometric learning, a technique derived from perceptual psychology. Our method leverages a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) and learns a hierarchical segmentation model using a psychometric learning framework. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, achieving competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods while using a fraction of the model size and computational resources. The proposed method is simple, efficient, and effective, making it suitable for real-world applications.

A deep learning based convolutional neural network (CNN) has been shown to achieve great performance for medical image segmentation. However, it remains a challenge to train such networks with limited training data. In this paper, we present a novel ensemble based deep CNN framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation, which is trained on both labeled and unlabeled data. Our framework utilizes an ensemble of CNNs to boost the segmentation performance. We adopt a weighted majority voting scheme to combine the outputs from individual CNNs, where the weights are learned from the labeled data. Furthermore, we introduce a novel data augmentation technique to generate more training samples from the unlabeled data.

Appearance contrast is a popular bottom-up cue used by visual attention models to simulate salient object segmentation, but it tends to produce fragmented saliency maps lacking global coherence, resulting in incorrect object identification. In this paper, we propose PISA, a method that improves the coherence of appearance-based saliency maps by taking advantage of two types of complementary contrast information: pixel-level and edge-level. PISA flexibly integrates different appearance contrast measures—such as intensity, color, and texture—with edge-preserving coherence modeling. We introduce a pixel-level contrast aggregation module that computes saliency from pixel-level contrasts, and an edge-level contrast aggregation module that computes saliency from edge-level contrasts. These two modules are subsequently combined to produce the final saliency map. We demonstrate via extensive experiments on common benchmarks that PISA consistently improves performance of saliency detection over strong baselines in terms of both accuracy and coherence, without any parameter tuning.

We study a system of two-color fermions in a cold and magnetized state in the mean-field approximation. By using the numerical linked-cluster expansion, we evaluate the thermodynamic potential for arbitrary values of the density and magnetization. For large values of the magnetization, the system undergoes a transition from a normal fluid to a Bose-Einstein condensate. On the other hand, for small values of the magnetization, the system stabilizes into a color superconducting state. By comparing the free energies for the different phases, we determine the boundary of the coexistence region between the normal fluid and the superconducting phases, and between the normal fluid and the Bose-Einstein condensate. We discuss the behavior of the order parameters and quasiparticle weights.

Model predictive control (MPC) is applied to a coupled tank liquid level system in this work. In this system, the liquid levels in two tanks, which are connected by a pipe, are controlled. The control objective is to transfer liquid from one tank to another while maintaining the liquid levels in both tanks at desired levels. The model of the system is derived using a mass balance approach on the liquid levels in the tanks. The controller is designed using a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) approach. The controller is tested on a set of realistic scenarios, and the results are compared with those obtained using a PID controller.

We present a general, lightweight system for accurate 3D medical image segmentation. Our system, called Network to Segment Them All (N2S2), is based on a single deep learning network that is capable of segmenting a wide variety of anatomical structures in 3D medical images. The network is designed to be efficient, with a small number of parameters and a low computational cost, making it suitable for use on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones or tablets.

 We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of 3D medical image datasets, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound images. Our results show that N2S2 is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of anatomical structures, including the brain, lungs, liver, and heart.

 We believe that N2S2 has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical image segmentation by providing a general and efficient solution that is capable of accurately segmenting a wide variety of anatomical structures in 3D medical images.

Recent progress in deep learning has enabled the development of powerful models for image semantic segmentation, i.e., assigning a label to each pixel in an image. However, these models are trained on large datasets and require a significant amount of computational resources, making them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a lightweight and efficient approach for image semantic segmentation based on personalized modeling. Our approach is designed to reduce the computational cost and memory requirements of the model, while still achieving high accuracy. We achieve this by combining a deep neural network with a set of personalized semantic prototypes, which are generated from a small number of labeled images. The personalized prototypes enable the model to adapt to new images with different semantics, and improve the segmentation accuracy by leveraging the user's knowledge and experience.

Recent advances in MRI acquisition enable scanning of the entire heart at once, making it possible to reconstruct a volumetric model of patient-specific cardiac chambers. This model can be used for help in surgical planning; however, it is challenging to manually segment the boundary of the cardiac chambers in the volume. We present a method for automatic segmentation of the left ventricle (LV) and right ventricle (RV) in cardiac MRI volumes using a transformer-based model. Our method reaches a F1 score of 0.91 on in-distribution testing data, and 0.80 on out-of-distribution data. In addition, our model generalizes to segment the RV in datasets where the RV was not present in the training data. We show that our model generalizes well to unseen datasets and out-of-distribution data in an open-world setting, despite only being trained on a fixed set of segments.

We present a new active contour model for image segmentation based on a generalized asymmetric dual-front approach. In this model, the interface is described by two fronts, one for the exterior and one for the interior of the object, which move simultaneously toward each other or away from each other depending on the local gradient direction. The front that is inside the evolving contour is always faster than the outside front. This feature imposes a strong constraint on the contour evolution, resulting in a bias toward the formation of a global contour that is closed and does not leak out of the object boundary. An important advantage of the proposed method is that it is very fast and easy to implement because it only involves a simple calculation of the gradient of the image and a marching process in the gradient direction. Experimental results on several segmentation benchmarks show the efficiency of the proposed approach compared with state-of-the-art active contour models.

We present a systematic approach to scene understanding for autonomous manipulation, leveraging recent advances in deep learning. In this work, we consider the task of picking objects from cluttered scenes, a key capability for autonomous robots. We introduce a novel deep architecture, termed Object-Context Embedding (OCE), that fuses object detection and semantic scene understanding. Our approach jointly reasons about the presence of objects, their contexts, and their interactions, enabling the robot to adapt its decisions to the scene at test-time. We show that our approach outperform state-of-the-art on the task of picking objects from scenes, measured by success rate and pick success. In particular, we achieve 79% pick success on the challenging Object Discovery and Learning (ODL) dataset, significantly improving upon the prior state of the art.

In this paper, we provide an overview of the most commonly used cardiac MR image segmentation techniques. We discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each technique and provide examples of their applications in clinical and research settings. We also discuss the future direction of cardiac MR image segmentation and potential applications in the clinic. The goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the current state of the art in cardiac MR image segmentation and to highlight its potential for improving the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease. We conclude that manual segmentation techniques have the advantage of producing high-quality segmentations but are highly time-consuming and require expertise. Automated techniques are a promising alternative with the advantage of being much faster and less expensive but suffer from the disadvantage of being less accurate.

We give a complete description of deformations of symmetric simple modular Lie (super)algebras with symmetric Cartan matrix. This extends results of Berglund–Hübner and Berglund–Zhu on deformations of symmetric simple Lie (super)algebras. The approach relies on a study of graded derivations of these algebras.

 Let $\g$ be a simple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, $D$ a full flag in $\g$, and $\Pi=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$ a basis of simple roots associated to $D$. Let $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r,\alpha_r+\alpha_{r+1},\dots,\alpha_r+\alpha_n\}$ be the associated simple system of roots. Assume that the Cartan matrix $A=(a_{ij})$, associated to $(\Delta,\Pi)$, is symmetric. Let $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathfrak{g}_\alpha$ be the corresponding symmetric simple Lie algebra.

We present a simple method to augment pretrained models with new anatomy and images, based on an in-depth analysis of the representations learned by the pretrained models. Our method is motivated by the observation that while pretrained models are trained on a diverse set of images, they learn highly specific representations, making them ineffective when used out of distribution. We find that this is because the representations learned are highly dependent on the presence of certain anatomy and that the absence of this anatomy often leads to the representations not being able to generalize well. Our method addresses this limitation by learning a new representation that can exploit both the information in the pretrained model as well as the new anatomy and images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different datasets: cardiac MRI, abdominal CT, and knee MRI. For all three datasets, we show that our method improves performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods, while requiring less labeled data.

Recent progress in deep learning has boosted the development of medical image segmentation models. However, most existing works focus on 2D images or 3D volumes without considering the inherent hierarchical structure of medical images. In this paper, we present a Pyramid Medical Transformer (PMT) to effectively exploit the pyramid structure of medical images for segmentation. Specifically, we design a Light-weight Attention Module (LAM) to capture the global and local information at different levels of the image pyramid. Moreover, to effectively integrate multi-scale information, we propose a Scale-aware Attention (SA) module that can focus on different scales of features adaptively. Furthermore, a Pyramid-aware Tokenization (PAT) strategy is proposed to selectively preserve the useful information from the low-level features for each token.

Head overcoat (HOC) thickness is an important diagnostic indicator for multiple sclerosis (MS), which can be automatically measured using magnetic resonance (MR) images. However, existing methods usually require additional manual corrections or optimizations, which is inconvenient for clinical use. In this paper, we propose a novel automatic HOC thickness measurement method based on deep learning. Our method is based on a NASNet-Large-Decoder net pre-trained on a large dataset of abdominal MR images. We fine-tune the pre-trained model on a small dataset of MS patients including T1-weighted (T1W), T2-weighted (T2W), and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images. The proposed method was validated on MS patients and healthy controls, and compared with two commonly used methods: manual drawing of regions of interest (ROIs) and an automatic method based on random forests (RFs).

Abstract— We present a framework for training a deep neural network for automated weed detection in aerial imagery with context. Our approach combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction with a support vector machine (SVM) for classification. The CNN is trained on a dataset of aerial images containing a variety of weeds and background contexts. The SVM is trained on the features extracted by the CNN from a separate dataset of images containing only weeds and background. Our approach achieves a high accuracy rate of 92.7% for weed detection in aerial imagery. Furthermore, our approach is able to detect weeds in imagery containing a variety of background contexts, such as fields, roads, and water bodies.

Recent interest in the control of magnetization dynamics has led to the development of new techniques for manipulating the magnetic properties of materials. In this study, we investigate the effect of interface anisotropy on the precession of magnetization initiated by laser heating. We find that a $\pi$ phase shift occurs in the precession of magnetization when the material is heated by a laser. This phase shift is a result of the interface anisotropy and the resulting change in the magnetic easy axis. We also find that the direction of the phase shift depends on the direction of the applied magnetic field, and that the phase shift can be controlled by the direction of the magnetic field. These findings could be useful for controlling the magnetic properties of materials and devices.

We present a novel falling-ball algorithm for image segmentation based on the minimization of a cost function via a simulated annealing approach. Our algorithm is inspired by the behavior of balls falling into a bowl of sand, where the sand is modeled as a smooth surface and the balls are initially placed on a grid overlaying the image. By iteratively moving the balls downward, the grid cells corresponding to the boundaries between regions in the image are gradually revealed. Our approach is able to handle a variety of segmentation scenarios and is particularly effective at segmenting images with complex and irregular boundaries. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm on a number of benchmark images and compare it to other state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. Our results show that our algorithm is able to produce high-quality segmentations that are comparable to or better than those produced by other algorithms, while being more efficient in terms of computation time.

An index is proposed to evaluate the validity of fuzzy-possibilistic C-means (FP-C) clustering. The index is calculated based on a similarity measure between the true data and the data classified by FP-C clustering. The proposed index gives a measure of the quality of clustering in terms of how well the clusters are defined by the data points they contain. The index ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating perfect clustering and 0 indicating no clustering. The validity index is compared to the fuzzy validity index (FVI) and the possibilistic validity index (PVI) for FP-C clustering. The results show that the proposed index is a good measure for evaluating the validity of FP-C clustering.

 Abstract:
We introduce SemSegLoss, a Python package providing a collection of state-of-the-art loss functions for training semantic segmentation models. It facilitates transfer learning and model evaluation by implementing popular loss functions associated with published semantic segmentation models. We include a carefully curated collection of readable and reproducible source code examples that span a wide range of publication settings and network architectures. This package simplifies the implementation life-cycle of semantic segmentation models, increases reproducibility in computer vision, and will continue to grow as a collaborative resource for the community. In this work, we conduct a thorough analysis of the package and examples, provide technical guidance on their usage, and outline future improvements.

Captions are a valuable source of information for semantic segmentation, despite most existing approaches treating them as auxiliary data or a weakly-supervised signal. In this paper, we investigate methods for harvesting information from captions for semantic segmentation. We propose a simple yet effective approach for utilizing captions in a weakly-supervised manner, by exploiting their temporal consistency and context information. Our key insight is that the caption for a given frame is likely to contain information about the presence and location of objects in that frame. We leverage this intuition to improve the performance of weakly-supervised semantic segmentation. Our approach consists of two main components: (1) a spatial attention module that uses the caption to focus on the relevant regions of the image, and (2) a temporal attention module that uses the caption to determine the relevance of different frames in a video.

Copula correlation is a novel dependence measure for continuous variables that overcomes the limitations of traditional measures such as Pearson's correlation. It provides a more accurate representation of the relationship between variables by measuring the equivalence of their cumulative distribution functions. This new measure has applications in various fields, including finance, insurance, and statistics. In this paper, we introduce copula correlation and demonstrate its advantages over existing dependence measures. We also extend Pearson's correlation to a new measure called copula-based correlation, which incorporates the copula correlation concept. This new measure is more flexible and can be applied to a wider range of variables than Pearson's correlation.

Most organisms use chemotaxis to detect and respond to chemical gradients, but collective decision-making processes that underpin swarm behaviour often appear to rely on other cues, such as mechanical signalling or social interactions. Here we show that collectively migrating locusts respond to odour gradients under laboratory conditions that minimise mechanical and social cues. We found that the chemotactic response of individuals was relatively poor, yet successful migration of the group relied on odour perception. We show that the locusts' aggregation behaviour emerges from the noise in individual responses, which is regulated by a transient amplification of responses to odour, probably caused by positive feedback between odour and behavioural states. Our results suggest that collective odour sensing can improve detection of odour gradients and provide the basis for reliable group navigation, despite individual responses being relatively poor. odour perception.

In this paper, we present a parameter decoupling strategy for semi-supervised 3D left atrium segmentation. Unlike most existing works that use a fully supervised approach, our method takes advantage of both supervised and unsupervised datasets for training. We argue that the inconsistency between the two datasets is mainly rooted in the parameter settings (e.g., initial starting points, threshold values, and regularization weights) rather than the network architecture itself. To tackle this issue, we propose a parameter decoupling strategy, in which we decouple the parameters into two parts: architecture parameters and appearance parameters. We then fine-tune the network separately on both supervised and unsupervised datasets, with the architecture parameters kept fixed. In this way, our method can effectively leverage the rich annotations from the supervised dataset and the abundant unlabeled samples from the unsupervised dataset, thereby achieving better performance in 3D left atrium segmentation.

A detailed and unified study of criteria for measures of quantum correlations is presented. After briefly reviewing the fundamental limitations on measuring correlations, we analyze in detail several recently proposed criteria for measures of quantum correlations. In contrast to previous studies, our analysis covers all major types of criteria, including those based on continuity, convexity, and contractivity conditions. We show that most of the recently proposed criteria are inherently weaker than others and derive general necessary and sufficient conditions for these criteria in terms of simple mathematical operations. We also present a new class of criteria that are applicable to any measure of quantum correlations and prove that they are all equivalent when the underlying measure is continuous, convex, and contractive. Finally, we give a complete description of all possible criteria for measures of quantum correlations and illustrate our results through several examples.

Toward panoptic segmentation, which directly predicts instance-level segmentation masks and instance labels for each pixel, we find that existing methods suffer from two limitations: (1) Most existing methods rely on post-processing steps that are expensive in terms of computational cost, and (2) Existing panoptic segmentation benchmarks include only coarse pixel-level ground truth, which hampers the training of dense prediction models. To address these issues, we present a simple but effective anchor-based approach for panoptic segmentation. By adapting the mask-scoring module in the detection framework, our method achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods while being much faster. In addition, to tackle the lack of dense ground truth, we present a new dataset, called , which has instance-level segmentation masks as ground truth. The proposed method achieves top performance on the and benchmarks, while being more than 2x faster than the next best method. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/panoptic-segmentation.

We introduce the notion of quasi-power law (QPL) ensembles, which are based on the idea of preserving the average properties of a power law ensemble (PLE) while modifying the tail of the distribution. We show that QPL ensembles are as resilient as PLEs to attacks that have been previously considered for PLEs, such as the birthday attack and the subset attack, while requiring a smaller key space. In addition, we show that QPL ensembles are useful for creating practical symmetric key generators, as they can be generated with a small number of bits and are highly resilient to attacks. We present a way to generate QPL ensembles that is based on a new method for generating PLEs, which is more efficient than the previously known methods.

 Introduction: Power law ensembles (PLEs) are a class of distributions that have been shown to be useful for creating practical symmetric key generators. A PLE is a distribution whose tail decay is proportional to a power law, which means that the probability of encountering a member of the ensemble decreases as a power law function of its rank in the ensemble.

We present a novel class of algorithms for submodular optimization that is both simpler and more powerful than previous methods. Our approach is based on reflecting the gradient of the objective function with respect to each decision variable. This reflection has two benefits: it simplifies the optimization problem by transforming it into a convex problem, and it exploits the structure of the submodular function to obtain a better approximation guarantee. Our reflection method can be easily incorporated into any first-order method, such as gradient descent or stochastic gradient descent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a wide variety of submodular optimization problems, including submodular function optimization, matroid intersection, and minimax optimization. We also show how to use our reflection method to solve the popular knapsack problem with fractional items, which has applications in numerous fields including robotics and finance.

A new approach to image segmentation based on the principal component analysis is presented. This approach is applied to the segmentation of in vitro cell colonies in bright field images. The individual cells are the basic elements for the segmentation, and therefore an appropriate estimation of cell regions is essential. In order to achieve this goal, a new filtering technique that utilizes the spatial dependence of the pixel intensity in the image is proposed. This technique, named as the self-guided filter, is used to preprocess the image, and the resulting image is then provided as the input to the proposed segmentation method. In this method, the image is decomposed into its principal components, and the segmentation is performed on the dominant principal component, which carries most of the useful information for segmentation.

We present a long-term visual localization system that utilizes semantic segmentations of the training images to improve performance. We pretrain a convolutional neural network (CNN) on the ImageNet dataset, and use the CNN to extract features from both the training and test images. We then use a support vector machine (SVM) to classify the images into 1000 fine-grained object classes. To segment the images, we propagate the activations of the last layer of the CNN through an iterative graph cuts algorithm. To localize a query image, we first classify the query image using the SVM, then we segment the query image using the trained segmentations from the training images, and finally we localize the query image by matching the segmented query image with the segmented training images. In addition, we implement several strategies to improve localization performance, including a prior based on the training images' geographic location information, and “in-session localization,” which utilizes object classes that are unique to the session to improve localization.

Medical image segmentation is prone to label corruption, which poses a severe impediment to clinical deployment. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of label corruption by learning a cross-denoising network (CDN) with a denoising branch and a correcting branch, aiming to restore clean labels for corrupted ones. Specifically, the denoising branch leverages the inherent smoothness of segmentations to remove noise, while the correcting branch focuses on the dissimilarity between the corrupted labels and their denoised versions to correct them. To effectively train the correcting branch, we introduce a domain shift adaptation module to align the distributions of uncorrupted and corrupted data, enabling the network to learn from both sources of data without leaking the clean labels to the corrupted side. We evaluate our method on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks with different degrees of label noise (20%, 40%, and 60%), and demonstrate its effectiveness against existing state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/CDN.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to 
cross-stain histopathology image segmentation based on a dual adaptive pyramid network (DAPNet). The DAPNet is composed of two adaptive pyramid networks (APNs), each designed to segment a specific stain in the histopathology image. The proposed method was tested on a dataset of 
histopathology images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project. The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and runtime.

 Introduction: 
Histopathology image segmentation refers to the process of identifying and classifying pixel regions in histopathology images based on the presence of specific stains. This process is crucial for accurate analysis and interpretation of histopathology images, which are widely used in medical diagnosis and research.

We propose a new method for the multiple testing problem under the regression setting. Our method is inspired by the rate optimal convergence rate of the lasso estimator. We derive the optimality in the sense that the expected number of false discoveries is minimized under a given power. We show that the projection pursuit, which is the basis of our method, achieves the optimal rate. We propose a multiple testing procedure that controls the false discovery rate (FDR) under the linear regression model with a potentially high-dimensional covariance matrix. The proposed method is motivated by the projection pursuit, a convex optimization technique, to search for the important variables.

We propose an alternative equation of motion approach to the single-impurity Anderson model based on a functional renormalization group scheme. By working directly with the correlation function, our approach provides a systematic and parameter-free way to take into account the frequency dependence of the self-energy. This allows us to investigate the spectral properties of the model at finite frequencies beyond the commonly used approximation of the frequency-independent self-energy. Within our approach, we derive an effective low-energy theory that captures the universal features of the model. We show that the self-energy obtained within our approach is consistent with the frequency-dependent self-energy obtained from the linearized Boltzmann equation of motion approach.

 Our approach provides a way to investigate the effects of the frequency-dependent self-energy on the spectral properties of the model.

Recent trends in renewable integration have brought about the need for advanced grid management technologies, with particular emphasis on distributed energy resources. Among other things, Inverse Power Flow (IPF) has been proposed as a promising solution for distributed energy resource management. In this paper, we provide an overview of the progress made so far on the IPF problem. We begin by introducing the basic concept of IPF and explain its advantages over the traditional power flow problem. We then review the various techniques that have been proposed to solve the IPF problem, including numerical methods, optimization-based methods, and heuristic methods. Finally, we discuss the future research directions for the IPF problem, including the need for more advanced modeling and solution techniques.

We present a comprehensive study on deep learning based cardiac MR image segmentation. Compared to state-of-the-art 2D approaches, 3D segmentation networks have shown promising results but at a significant increase in computational cost and without a noticeable improvement in performance. Our exploration of current 2D and 3D techniques reveals that 2D models perform poorly on long-axis slices, which contain valuable information for segmentation. We resolve this issue by proposing a simple yet effective approach that enforces 2D models to output 3D segmentation results. With this approach, we achieve better performance than 2D-only and 3D-only models on long-axis slices while keeping the computational requirements of 2D models. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of popular data augmentation techniques on model performance.

Recent progresses in semantic segmentation mainly focus on modeling the spatial information within a video frame for accurate pixel-level prediction. Despite the temporal nature of the problem, where the objects of interest undergo motion and appearance changes, existing methods tend to overlook such spatio-temporal information, which could provide valuable cues for improved performance. In this paper, we propose a novel approach, namely STD2P (Spatio-Temporal Data-Driven Pooling), to effectively incorporate spatio-temporal information for semantic segmentation. Specifically, we introduce a novel spatio-temporal pooling module that can capture the dynamic properties of the objects of interest in an effective and learnable manner. In addition, we propose a spatio-temporal attentive pooling module that can selectively focus on the regions with distinct motion properties. The proposed approach exhibits state-of-the-art performance on both the NYU Depth V2 and KITTI datasets, significantly improving upon the previous state-of-the-art methods.

We present a deep learning framework for joint shape learning and segmentation of medical images. Our method leverages a minimalistic deep network architecture that is low-cost in memory and computational requirements, making it suitable for clinical deployment. We introduce a novel shape prior encoded into the network via a shape-conditioned loss function that promotes consistent object boundaries across image slices. Furthermore, our method combines expert-labeled and self-supervised shape priors into a single framework to overcome the limited availability of expert-labeled training data. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on the problem of left-atrium segmentation from cardiac MR images. In comparison to related methods, our approach achieves a significantly higher segmentation quality while maintaining a low computational cost.

Generative Models are typically trained under strong assumptions: 3D object categories are assumed to have a large number of object instances, and those instances are assumed to be ordered, e.g., sorted by their horizontal pose. We question these assumptions in the context of arranging object instances in a horizontal strip: How many instances can be recovered, if at all, when there are no ordering constraints? If ordering is imposed, how much does it help, and how much supervision is required? We investigate the limits of generative modeling under various supervisory signals, ranging from ordering constraints (e.g., horizontal pose) to no supervision at all. Our analysis reveals that while fully-supervised models perform well when the number of instances is large, they struggle when the number of instances is small or when the instances are even partially ordered. In contrast, our proposed method, GENESIS-V2, which does not rely on iterative refinement, performs consistently across all settings, often outperforming the state-of-the-art.

We explore the feasibility of using social media data from Twitter to predict intraday changes in exchange rates. Our hypothesis is that Twitter sentiment can predict the direction of exchange rate movements. We find that sentiment is a leading indicator of exchange rate changes and that positive sentiment has a greater forecasting power for appreciating exchange rates compared to negative sentiment for depreciating rates. We also explore the theory that the tone of tweets may be related to the level of uncertainty in the market and find some support for this theory. Additionally, we find that the predictive power of sentiment varies across different currencies, and that the level of impact of Twitter sentiment is highest for the Canadian dollar, followed by the British pound, and then the euro. Our results suggest that social media data can be a valuable tool for predicting intraday exchange rate movements.

Let S be a finite set of points in the plane no three of which are collinear. An dominating set T for S is a subset of S such that every point of S is reachable from at least one point of T. The dominating set problem asks whether there is a dominating set of a given size for S. This problem is NP-complete. In this paper, we propose a linear kernel for the dominating set problem on planar point sets. Our kernel has size O(n^{1/2+eps}), where n is the number of points in S and eps is an arbitrarily small constant. This improves upon the previously best known kernel with O(n) size.

Recent developments in transformation optics have enabled the possibility of creating materials with interesting and potentially useful optical properties. These so-called 'metamaterials' are engineered to have properties not found in nature, such as negative refraction or the ability to bend light around objects, making them appear invisible. One property that has not yet been achieved in metamaterials is the creation of 'anti-telephones', or materials that have closed null geodesics, allowing light to travel in a loop without escaping the material. In this paper, we explore the possibility of creating anti-telephones in metamaterials using a novel approach involving the introduction of 'seeding defects'. Our results show that it is possible to create anti-telephones in metamaterials, with the seeding defects playing a crucial role in the formation of closed null geodesics. We also investigate the optical properties of these anti-telephones and find that they exhibit a number of interesting behaviors, including the ability to generate multiple images and the potential for applications in optical computing.

We propose a hybrid mmWave and camera system for long-range depth imaging. The system simultaneously captures a mmWave image and a camera image, and then fuses the two types of data for long-range depth estimation. In the mmWave image, depth information is encoded in the phase information of the pixels. A depth estimation algorithm is then applied to the mmWave image to obtain a preliminary depth map. The camera image is used to refine the preliminary depth map obtained from the mmWave image. Furthermore, we introduce a novel depth estimation algorithm that consists of an iterative refinement process.

Recent progress in medical image segmentation has largely been achieved by leveraging large institutional datasets. However, such efforts suffer from dataset heterogeneity, inhibiting the generalization of learned models across institutions and resulting in poor performance on datasets outside the training distribution. In this paper, we propose FedDG, a flexible framework for learning robust segmentors via federated domain generalization (FedDG). FedDG leverages episodic learning, a technique inspired by human cognitive learning, to model distributions in continuous frequency space. We demonstrate that our model can learn robust segmentors from only a few institutional contributions, resulting in improved performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets. We showcase the efficacy of our approach on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, yielding state-of-the-art performance with trained models that are over 200 times smaller.

In this paper, we propose a topological image segmentation technique based on the topological derivative for automatic recognition of sign language. In order to segment the input hand gesture sequences from the video sequences, we adopt the watershed transformation to obtain the topological derivative of the gradient magnitude of the video frames. Since the gradient magnitude does not satisfy the assumption of the topological derivative, we apply an isotropic filter to obtain a suitable input for the watershed transformation. The use of isotropic filter prevents the gradient from being dominated by few directions and makes the watershed based segmentation technique more effective and robust. The segmented regions are then subjected to a classification based on the statistical features extracted from the normalized RGB histogram of the regions. In the next stage, a feature selection based on the Fisher score is applied to reduce the dimensionality and to obtain a set of features that are most relevant to the classification task.

Recent advances in few-shot learning have achieved remarkable performance in image classification tasks, but have not been extensively explored for medical image segmentation, which is a fundamental but challenging task in medical imaging analysis. In this paper, we present a semi-supervised few-shot learning approach for medical image segmentation. Our approach is based on a novel few-shot learning framework that combines semi-supervised learning and few-shot learning, which we call semi-supervised few-shot learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in few-shot learning and semi-supervised learning.

 Our approach has two main components. The first component is a novel few-shot learning framework that combines semi-supervised learning and few-shot learning.

Extraction of gray image from a color image is very important and it is the first step of extraction process in any image processing application. A new approach is proposed to extract the gray image using fuzzy logic. In this paper, RGB components of color image are considered as input for fuzzy system. These inputs are fuzzified and processed by fuzzy logic to obtain a single output which is the gray value corresponding to that pixel. The proposed method is tested on various images and results are also compared with existing methods. The proposed method produced better results in terms of contrast and brightness.

We propose a robust regression method for image binarization under heavy noises and nonuniform background. In image binarization, the regression function is trained to predict the binary threshold for each pixel given the pixel intensity. Existing regression methods are usually affected by heavy noises and nonuniform background, as the training data are usually contaminated by these factors and the regression function is not able to adapt to these variations. In this paper, we propose a robust regression method which can adapt to these variations and improve the performance of image binarization. The proposed method consists of two steps. The first step is to train a robust regression function using the robust loss function, which is able to adapt to heavy noises and nonuniform background.

We continue our study of the global Fukaya category begun in our previous paper [18]. After briefly recalling the definition of the global Fukaya category, we discuss various examples, including singular connections and vanishing cycles, and explain how they relate to our definition. We then prove a technical result on functoriality of the global Fukaya category with respect to a bijection on the set of exact Lagrangian submanifolds, which generalizes a result of Abouzaid and Smith [7]. Finally, we give several examples of computations of the global Fukaya category in the case of affine manifolds, and explain how to use our functoriality result to establish an isomorphism in the case of affine bundles.

Recent progress in segmentation algorithms driven by large-scale annotated image datasets has advanced the state-of-the-art in medical image analysis. However, manual annotation work is costly and time-consuming, which hinders the generalization performance of deep learning models in medical image analysis tasks, especially when only a small amount of annotated data is available. In this paper, we present a cooperative training strategy with latent space data augmentation (COLA) to enhance the generalization performance of deep learning models for medical image segmentation. Compared with conventional data augmentation methods, COLA introduces few-shot segmentation labels into the latent space of a pre-trained segmentation model to generate more diverse augmented samples for training. We implement COLA on three public breast histopathology image datasets with different annotation sizes. Results show that our method significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art segmentation models in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness, especially when only a small amount of annotated data is available.

We present a novel approach for semantic image segmentation based on a supervised learning framework. Our method is based on a regularized convolutional neural network (CNN) that is designed to preserve object boundaries and prevent over-segmentation. The key component of our approach is a novel fully-connected layer that is added to the end of a pre-trained CNN. This layer takes as input the output of the final convolutional layer and produces a segmentation map as output. The fully-connected layer is designed to minimize an energy function that enforces a regularization term based on a novel boundary-preserving loss function. This regularization term is designed to encourage the network to produce segmentation maps that accurately delineate object boundaries.

This paper proposes an unsupervised image segmentation method based on global and local criteria optimization. It consists in minimizing an energy function which takes into account both gradient and similarity terms through a Bayesian network. This network models the spatial dependence between pixels, and allows the use of various criteria at different scales. We perform an iterative optimization of the energy function, which alternately minimizes a gradient descent and a similarity term. The optimization of the latter is performed by propagating evidence through the Bayesian network. This method does not require any initialization or parameter tuning, and allows to obtain competitive results compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods, while being simpler and faster.

We present TernausNet, a U-Net variant designed for efficient implementation, while retaining the ability to effectively segment instance levels of intra-class variability. The design includes a VGG11 encoder, pre-trained on ImageNet, that is modified for semi-supervised segmentation. We modify the encoder by adding a convolutional layer with a ReLU activation function and a convolutional layer with a sigmoid activation function. These modifications enable the encoder to produce segmentation masks with well-defined boundaries. We evaluate TernausNet on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and achieve F1 scores of 95.4% and 92.1% on the val sets, respectively. Our code and model weights are available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/segmentation.

Recent works have shown that fully convolutional networks (FCNs) trained for medical image synthesis tasks such as lesion segmentation can be utilized as effective data augmentation tools. However, directly applying FCNs to anatomical regions-of-interest (RoIs) may result in significant structural alterations due to the lack of global anatomical context in the cropped regions. In this paper, we present an approach to adapt FCNs for effective data augmentation without losing the overall structural integrity of the medical images. Our key insight is that the network can be designed to learn and restore the underlying structural information of the medical images in a fully convolutional manner. To this end, we propose a structure-preserving fully convolutional network (SynNet) architecture consisting of two modules: a structure-aware module and a synthesis module. Given a lesion-mapped atlas, the structure-aware module precisely estimates the underlying anatomical structure in the RoI, while the synthesis module produces the final synthesized lesion map.

We present a new computational method for multivariate Bayesian image segmentation (MBIS) based on a hierarchical Bayesian model that we developed for segmenting images obtained from multivariate fluorescent microscopy images. In our approach, we define a joint distribution that models the spatial continuity across pixels within each segment and the relationship between multiple fluorescent channels. We introduce a novel algorithm, called the Markov chain Monte Carlo proposal generator (MCPMG), for efficient sampling of this joint distribution. The MCPMG combines the benefits of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, which provide robust Bayesian inference for high-dimensional models, with proposal-based sampling techniques that introduce a form of local exploration, enabling more efficient segmentation. The resulting MBIS algorithm is demonstrated on both simulated and real data. The simulated data include scenarios that are designed to be challenging for existing algorithms, involving a high degree of non-linear intensity variations and noise.

Linear radiofrequency (RF) ion traps have become a key component in many areas of experimental physics, notably for the realization of quantum computers, but also for fundamental studies of ion dynamics and surface interactions. Despite their broad use, a detailed understanding of ion transport in these traps remains elusive. In this article, we use numerical simulations to investigate ion transport in macroscopic RF linear traps, characterized by electrode voltages and trap parameters typically used in experiments. By varying an external electric field along the trap, we observe the transport of single ions through the trap, characterized by a mobility edge and a threshold for ion transport. We show that the position of these thresholds depends on system parameters such as the RF frequency and the static electric field magnitude. By investigating the influence of system parameters on our ability to transport ions against a static electric field, we derive criteria for efficient ion transport in RF linear traps.

Resources allocation aims to distribute limited resources efficiently among users to maximize the overall utility. In this paper, we consider the resource allocation problem for multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar with multiple targets for non-coherent localization. We propose a novel algorithm that allocates resources based on the channel gain and the location of the targets. The algorithm maximizes the overall probability of detection and localization of all targets by allocating resources to the strongest channel and distributing the remaining resources among the other channels. We also derive a lower bound on the probability of detection and localization for comparison. The simulation results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the lower bound and other resource allocation strategies.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic segmentation of pelvic magnetic resonance (MR) images. Our method combines pyramid pooling and attention mechanism to capture both global and local information. We first apply pyramid pooling to extract multi-scale features from the input images. Then, we employ an attention mechanism to weigh the importance of different features for accurate segmentation. The proposed method was evaluated on a public dataset consisting of pelvic MR images. The experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed.

Current techniques for automated labeling of cardiac MR images are often not accurate enough for clinical use. In this paper, we propose a method for improving the accuracy of automated labeling. Our method is based on the fusion of labels from multiple atlases, using a neural network to combine the labels. We show that our method is effective in improving the accuracy of automated labeling, and that it is able to generalize to images that are not included in the training set.


 Our method, which we call Neural Multi-Atlas Label Fusion, combines labels from multiple atlases, with a neural network that is trained on a set of training images. The neural network learns to combine the labels from the atlases in a way that is optimal for the training images.

Recent progress in image collage generation has largely focused on unconditional methods that apply random transformations to images, followed by optimization of a collage objective. In this work, we revisit the paradigm of collage optimization and propose an approach that transforms image sets by attending to memory of previously seen images, while iteratively generating a collage. We introduce a new memory-based loss that encourages the preservation of memorized image features in the generated collage, and a memory attentive loss that further enforces memorization of recent images. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset of image sets, where each set is composed of a guiding image and context images related to the same scene. We show that our method, when applied to the generation of image collages from sets of images, either with or without the guiding image, consistently improves upon the state of the art in collage generation. Our code is released at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/ImageCollage.

We present a multi-task learning framework, DeepSaliency, for joint training of a deep neural network (DNN) for image saliency detection and for learning the underlying salient object characteristics. Our method learns a shared deep representation between the two tasks: predicting saliency maps and predicting object masks in salient regions. We introduce a novel salient object characteristic mining loss that enforces the DNN to learn a deep representation that can be used to selectively mine salient object characteristics. Our method also naturally leverages an ensemble of predicted object masks for robustly segmenting salient objects. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on four publicly available datasets, comparing to the state-of-the-art methods on both saliency detection and salient object segmentation. In particular, our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance on the MIT-CBCL and UCFSports datasets with a significant margin.

We present an image segmentation algorithm that recursively partitions an image into foreground and background regions using a sparse subset selection approach. Our algorithm is inspired by the observation that, in digital images, pixels belonging to different objects are usually not all connected. Therefore, instead of relying on a dense labeling, we aim to find a sparse subset of pixels that can effectively partition the image into separate components. To this end, we define a novel cost function that encourages spatial coherence within each segment, as well as distinguishes between foreground and background pixels. We solve the resulting optimization problem using an efficient graph cuts algorithm, which iteratively selects a sparse subset of pixels to partition the image until convergence. The proposed algorithm is fully automatic, parameter-free, and fast, making it suitable for many real-world applications.

Many works in computer vision have applied data augmentation for training models that generalize to unseen domains. In this paper, we question whether data augmentation is always needed for good generalization. surpris-ingly, we find that for some datasets with synthetic data, data augmentation can even hurt model generalization. We show that this is because the augmentation is already implicitly inside the data generation process, rendering the standard data augmentation procedure unnecessary and even detrimental. Based on this insight, we propose a simple data preprocessing method that removes the augmentation from the training data, and demonstrates improved generalization performance on both synthetic and real-world data. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/FinSAIGeneration.

In this paper, we present a teacher-student framework with an attention module for semi-supervised medical image segmentation from mixed supervision. We train a teacher model using only labeled images, and then use the pre-trained teacher model to generate pseudo labels for unlabeled images. We propose an attention module to weigh the importance of different information for segmentation. We optimize the student model with both labeled and pseudo labeled data, and the proposed attention module further improves the segmentation performance. In addition, we investigate the use of multiple teachers for the purpose of knowledge transfer. The experimental results on three different public lung segmentation benchmarks, using mixed supervision of CT and MRI scans, show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

Recent progress in image segmentation is significantly advanced by the 3D model assisted approach, which utilizes a 3D model to provide prior knowledge for the segmentation task. Given a query image and a set of 3D models, the goal is to find the optimal 3D model which best explains the query image. However, the existing 3D model assisted methods usually assume that the surface of the 3D model is composed of a finite number of segments, which is not suitable for scanning objects with complex surfaces, where significant texture variations and geometric structures usually exist in a single segment. In this paper, we propose a new 3D model assisted image segmentation method to overcome the above limitations. The key idea is to formulate the segmentation problem as a non-parametric binary labeling problem on the surface of the 3D model, and then solve it using a conditional random field (CRF) model. To efficiently compute the CRF energy, we propose a new algorithm called the multi-scale graph cut algorithm, which approximates the CRF energy by a graph cut energy on a multi-scale graph structure.

We present an implementation of discontinuous Galerkin methods for solving shallow water equations on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). Our implementation uses a non-conservative formulation of the shallow water equations, which enables us to develop a straightforward and efficient solver on the GPU. We utilize the compute capability of GPUs to solve the resulting linear system of equations arising from the discretization of the non-conservative form. To handle the non-linear terms in the shallow water equations, a nonlinear solver is employed. We use a simple iterative linear solver for this purpose. The performance of our solver is evaluated on several test cases, and the results are compared with those obtained from a CPU-based solver.

Medical image segmentation is an active research field, producing a large variety of methods and a vast amount of published works. Compared to other medical image processing tasks, the field of segmentation is particularly challenging since it requires methods to correctly classify voxels or pixels in a large variety of shapes present in different medical images. Among the different approaches to address this problem, a particular class of methods relies on using loss functions that are able to leverage available information in the form of a prior. In these methods, the network is trained to classify pixels or voxels together with a confidence value measuring the reliability of the predicted class. This confidence value is then used to compute the final segmentation mask, where pixels or voxels with a confidence value above a certain threshold are considered part of the foreground, while the others are assigned to the background. In this paper, we provide an extensive survey on this class of prior-based loss functions for medical image segmentation.

We introduce MeanShift++, a variant of the classic MeanShift algorithm for visual object detection and tracking. Like its predecessor, MeanShift++ uses a weighted average of the feature values in the detection window to model the posterior probability distribution. However, MeanShift++ changes the weighting scheme to improve the algorithm's ability to find objects that are spatially localized, poorly differentiated, or smaller than the search window. To evaluate MeanShift++, we implemented tracking and segmentation variants of the algorithm and compared them to their MeanShift counterparts on six widely used benchmark datasets for visual object tracking and segmentation. In all cases, we observed a significant improvement in accuracy and speed with no increase in running time.

 MeanShift has recently emerged as an extremely fast and efficient alternative to more complex methods for tracking objects in videos and segmenting objects in images.

An image segmentation method based on a contrario selection of optimal partitions is presented. The method aims to find a good compromise between the segmentation accuracy and the number of segments generated. It is based on a genetic algorithm that selects pixels to optimize an energy function. In contrast to most previous work on genetic image segmentation, the algorithm searches for a good segmentation without any a priori constraint on the number of segments. Instead, it searches for the optimal segmentation in an unbounded solution space. An evaluation of the method on several images shows that it is very efficient in finding a good segmentation that closely approximates the optimal segmentation.

Recent works on semantic biomedical image segmentation have achieved promising results. However, most of these methods focus on segmenting single-modality images or only a limited number of modalities. Moreover, these methods usually segment images independently without exploiting the correlations among the multiple modalities. In this paper, we present an approach to semantic biomedical image segmentation that addresses these limitations. Our approach consists of two steps: (1) a novel task decomposition method that decomposes the segmentation of a pair of correlated modalities into a set of independent subtasks, and (2) an effective synchronization mechanism that utilizes the correlations among the subtasks to improve the segmentation results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different datasets: ISBI 2017 Cardiac MRI Segmentation Challenge, IXI dataset, and Medseg dataset.

We introduce the notion of height for piecewise-testable (PT) languages, generalizing the concept of width for regular languages. Given an alphabet of size n, a PT language L has height at most h if each characteristic word of L has length at most h, and L is infinite otherwise. We show that for every infinite PT language L over an alphabet of size n, there is an equivalent PT language of height at most n. This result implies that the height of PT languages is unbounded when the alphabet size is unbounded. We also show that the height of PT languages is strictly smaller than the width of regular languages, thus providing another perspective on the difference between the two classes. Furthermore, we prove that the height of a PT language is equal to the maximum height of its syntactic congruence classes, generalizing a result about the width of regular languages. We investigate the complexity of the logic of subword concatenations, which is a fragment of first-order logic capturing PT languages.

We present HyperDense-Net, a densely connected Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for multi-modal image segmentation. It leverages recent advances in CNN architecture design to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the 2015 Multi-Modal Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) Challenge. A novel feature of our approach is its use of a densely connected CNN architecture, whereby each layer in the network is connected to every other layer, rather than just the immediately preceding layer. This allows the network to learn complex, hierarchical representations of the input data, which proved critical for performance on the BraTS 2015 dataset. We evaluate our approach on the BraTS 2015 validation and test datasets and achieve a weighted intersection over union (IoU) of 0.8314 and 0.7981, respectively, ranking first in the challenge. Code and models are available at https://github.com/HyperDense-Net/HyperDense-Net.

Recent progress in image segmentation is largely driven by large-scale supervised learning with abundant labeled data. However, in many real-world applications, obtaining abundant labeled data is difficult, and a supervised learning paradigm is therefore insufficient. In this paper, we present a new framework that leverages not only labeled data but also other modalities (e.g., unlabeled images and point clouds) for image segmentation. We disentangle the shared and individual information among different modalities to achieve segmentation by aligning and fusing the disentangled information. The key challenge lies in the unlabeled images and point clouds, which may contain severe misalignment and large domain gaps. To handle it, we propose a novel geometric alignment method to establish a coherent feature space across different modalities.

We present a real-time multi-object tracking (MOT) system that is trained entirely in a category-agnostic manner, i.e., without any category-specific bounding box labels whatsoever. Despite this, our system performs comparably with state-of-the-art MOT methods on the MOT17 benchmark, while being significantly more general and flexible. In particular, our method achieves ~80% MOT accuracy (mAP) on MOT17, compared to ~64% achieved by the current literature. Furthermore, we achieve this without any use of ground truth bounding boxes during training, or any other kind of strong supervision. To achieve these results, we leverage a recently proposed object tracker called Generalized Association (GA) that is trained using only image-level labels. We then show that GA is actually equivalent to a network that combines a Siamese Network with a one-shot detector (SSD), and use this observation to improve GA's tracking performance.

In this paper, we present a new image segmentation method based on active contours without edges. Unlike the original active contour without edges model, we propose to use a regional active contour model, which can handle the ambiguity of the initial contour placement in the image without edges. Our method is based on the variational level set framework, in which we introduce a new energy functional combining both the regional and the traditional smoothness terms. The regional term encourages the contour to partition the image into spatially coherent regions, while the smoothness term enforces the contour to be smooth and compact. To optimize the energy functional, we propose to use a new gradient descent algorithm which is specifically designed to handle the regional term. In order to improve the efficiency of our method, we introduce a machine learning component to approximate the regional term in the energy functional.
