We introduce a general framework for joint boundary-aware segmentation and cutout, which can be applied to both indoor and outdoor scenes, for mobile and web applications. It is the first approach to simultaneously estimate objects and their boundaries in a feed-forward manner. A boundary-aware segmentation network (BoaNet) is developed to predict object boundaries and segment objects in an end-to-end trainable fashion. In the BoaNet, a novel boundary-aware skip connection is proposed to couple the feature representations of fine and coarse scales, forcing the network to focus on both the object regions and their boundaries in an explicit manner. Furthermore, we propose a cutout augmentation method to train the BoaNet, which can not only improve the generalization performance but also enhance the diversity of the training data. When tested on four benchmark datasets, the BoaNet yields state-of-the-art results.

Deep learning has been demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in various computer vision tasks, including image segmentation. However, whether deep learning is the best choice for image segmentation remains questionable. This paper compares deep learning-based image segmentation with other classical image segmentation methods, including edge-based segmentation, region-based segmentation, and hybrid methods, on various metrics. To perform a fair comparison, the same evaluation metrics and data sets are used for all methods. The comparison results reveal that deep learning-based methods perform better in terms of accuracy but not in terms of runtime. Furthermore, the state-of-the-art deep learning-based methods do not outperform classical methods by a large margin, which questions whether deep learning is necessary for image segmentation.

Deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for medical image segmentation, enabling the development of accurate and automated methods for extracting meaningful information from medical images. This paper provides an overview of the current state of deep learning for medical image segmentation and discusses the challenges and opportunities in this field. We first introduce the concept of deep learning and its application to medical image segmentation. We then review the most commonly used deep learning architectures for medical image segmentation, including fully connected networks, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks. We then discuss the challenges of training deep learning models on medical image data, including the lack of large, labeled datasets and the need for domain-specific knowledge. We finally discuss the opportunities for future research in this field, including the potential for transfer learning and multi-task learning to improve the performance of deep learning models for medical image segmentation.

Recent developments in space propulsion have opened up the possibility of using nuclear electric or solar electric propulsion for interplanetary missions. These methods have higher efficiency than the traditional chemical propulsion methods, leading to shorter transfer times. We compare four different space propulsion methods using parameters relevant to a crewed Mars mission: nuclear electric, solar electric, nuclear thermal, and chemical propulsion. We consider the effects of reduced thrust levels on transfer time, mass, and complexity of the missions. We find that nuclear electric and solar electric propulsion can reduce the transfer time by half a year or more compared to chemical propulsion, despite having lower thrust levels. We also find that the nuclear electric method has a lower mass compared to the other methods, while the solar electric method has the lowest complexity.

We introduce a novel framework for parsing freehand sketches composed of line drawings and composed shapes. We tackle the parsing problem in the wild, where the shapes and their compositions in the sketch are not predefined and can take any form. To this end, we design a deep fully convolutional neural network that directly predicts a pixel-wise labeling of the sketch, treating the parsing problem as a pixel-level classification task. This approach allows our network to be parse-free, in that it does not require training examples of specific parsings of the sketch. In order to handle the variability and ambiguity of sketches in the wild, we propose a new architecture, SFSegNet, which is based on dilated fully convolutional networks and incorporates both shape and composition cues within a single architecture. We validate our approach on the public SketchParse dataset and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

We report on electrical transport measurements through few-layer graphene/boron-nitride/few-layer graphene structures with encapsulated boron-nitride (h-BN) layers, as a function of graphene layer number and gate voltage. In contrast to most transport studies on few-layer graphene, we do not rely on the availability of sharp graphene contacts, nor on an interaction with the substrate. This allows us to study few-layer graphene transport in a setup optimized for cleanliness and isolation from contaminants and the substrate, thus probing the intrinsic few-layer graphene properties. By studying the evolution of the quantum Hall effect as a function of layer number, we determine the layer-dependent charge neutrality levels of few-layer graphene. We observe a clear signature of the formation of a gate-tunable band gap in the monolayer and bilayer cases. Our results provide insight into the layer-dependent physics of few-layer graphene, and evidence for a gate-tunable band gap in these systems.

Efficient 2D neuron boundary segmentation is a fundamental step in 3D reconstruction of neuron structures from confocal microscopy images. We propose a method to exploit local topological constraints, which are inherent in neuron structures, to achieve better segmentation results. By modeling the topological constraints with a Markov Random Field, our approach produces accurate segmentations even in challenging regions where other approaches can fail. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of synthetic images and compare it with state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms. Our approach achieves significant improvements in segmentation accuracy and efficiency, with an average increase of 5% in F1-score and a speedup of 50% in runtime.

 Our method is inspired by the observation that neuron boundaries are often locally connected and have a tree-like structure, with smaller branches branching off larger branches.

In this paper, we propose a new method for finger vein recognition. Our method generates code representing vein patterns of a finger captured by a camera. The code is generated by quantizing the vein patterns into multiple levels of binary codes. To recognize a user, we match the code of the input image with the code of a registered image. We evaluate the performance of our method using a public finger vein database. The result shows that our method achieves a high recognition rate with a low false acceptance rate.

Recent works in semantic segmentation have demonstrated the potential of learning from weakly-annotated data when a limited number of training images are annotated by a small number of unreliable and inconsistent labels. However, existing methods usually assume that the uncertainty is induced only by the limited training data and fail to model the uncertainty coming from the variability of the annotator, which is particularly significant in the case of few/no-training-data settings. In this paper, we argue that the spatial smoothness prior learned from the reliable regions should not be too strong when the reliability of the annotations starts to degrade. We introduce a spatially varying label smoothing (SVLS) approach to capture the uncertainty from annotator variability in semantic segmentation. Specifically, given the initial annotations, we estimate the reliability map that indicates the level of confidence in the annotations. Then, we spatially adjust the label smoothing strength according to the reliability map.

Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in urban driving perception, and directly affects the performance of subsequent applications. However, existing works usually rely on specific datasets, causing low generalization performance on new datasets. In this paper, we present a universal semantic segmentation framework for fisheye urban driving images, named FUSION, which is trained on one dataset and can be directly applied to any other dataset with no fine-tuning. The framework is built upon a consolidated fisheye training pipeline, where a geometric distortion module and a dataset-specific refinement module are sequentially applied. Within the pipeline, a generic network is designed to adapt to various datasets by refining the outputs of different geometric distortion modules, which are uniquely determined by the characteristics of the datasets, such as the field-of-view and image resolution. We evaluate our method on three standard fisheye urban driving image datasets with different image sizes and fields-of-view.

Recent advances in medical imaging technology have resulted in a vast amount of labeled medical images from different domains, posing challenges for traditional medical image analysis approaches that are designed to specific domains. In this paper, we present a novel unsupervised domain adaptation framework for medical image segmentation. It selectively adapts the source domain (e.g., CT) to the target domain (e.g., MRI) by leveraging the structural similarity between the domains and the similarity in the annotations of the images. Specifically, we propose to optimize an objective function that minimizes the segmentation error on the target domain while keeping the structural similarity between the source and target domains. The proposed method is evaluated on four different public available abdominal organ segmentation datasets (CT and MRI) with different sizes. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.

Recent results in semantic segmentation, especially in biomedical imaging, have been driven by large-scale annotated datasets. However, annotating dense pixel-level labels is expensive, and for some applications, the availability of trained experts to perform the annotation is limited. We introduce a new paradigm called DSAL: Deeply Supervised Active Learning from Strong and Weak Labelers, that aims to minimize the amount of annotation required for training, while learning a model that performs no worse than the baseline that uses all the labels. In DSAL, a weak annotator performs initial annotation, and a strong annotator cleans up the errors of the weak annotator. This cleaning process generates strongly supervised training examples in a semi-supervised active learning setting. We show that this training paradigm is effective for training deep learning models for biomedical image segmentation, and that the resulting models perform competitively with respect to models trained with all the labels.

Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in the United States, affecting more than 2.7 million people. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is an effective treatment for AFib; however, approximately 20% of patients experience postoperative recurrence. It is critical to identify patients at high risk of recurrence after RFA for targeted medical therapy. This study proposes a deep learning-based approach to estimate postoperative AFib recurrence using standard 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs).

 A total of 167 patients who underwent RFA for symptomatic drug-refractory AFib between August 2016 and July 2020 were included in this study. For each patient, the standard 12-lead ECG recorded on the first postoperative day was used for model training and validation.

We present infrared (IR) spectral observations of the nearby active galactic nucleus (AGN) Arp 220 undertaken with the Infrared Space Observatory (ISO) and the Spitzer Space Telescope. The IR spectral energy distributions (SEDs) are characterized by strong emission from hot dust, with the 12 and 25 μm emission being particularly pronounced. There are also clear indications of emission from the AGN power source in the mid-IR, but this emission component is comparatively much weaker. We find that the dust spectral energy distribution between 8 and 12 μm can be described using a modified black body with relative wavelength dependence characterized by α_V = −1.1 ± 0.1. This value is consistent with those obtained for other AGN and is markedly different from the value of α_V = +1.7 obtained from the Rayleigh-Jeans tail of the stellar black body.

Recent progress in deep learning allows training models to translate between different domains, such as image style transfer and point cloud-to-image translation. However, most existing works focus on preserving the object structure or the geometry of the objects without considering the semantic meanings of the objects. In this paper, we tackle the problem of multi-modal domain translation from LiDAR point clouds to panoramic color images, which enables us to preserve both the geometry and the semantics of the objects in the translated images. Specifically, we propose a novel framework that consists of two components: a geometry-aware translator and a semantics-aware translator. The geometry-aware translator aims to capture the geometric structure of the objects and the spatial layout of the scene, while the semantics-aware translator aims to capture the object categories and their part relationships. To train the two components, we propose a new loss function that combines the geometry-aware loss and the semantics-aware loss into a unified framework.

Superpixel segmentation is a fundamental step for many computer vision applications. In this paper, we present an efficient superpixel segmentation approach based on dynamic and iterative spanning forests. Our method leverages the benefits of both pixel-level and region-level information, combining the advantages of traditional pixel-based segmentation techniques and recent region-based methods. Specifically, we iteratively construct a spanning forest over an evolving graph, where each node represents a pixel and each edge encodes appearance and spatial similarities between neighboring pixels. By dynamically updating the spanning forest at each iteration, our method is able to capture the gradual convergence of the segmentation process. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art superpixel segmentation methods.

We propose a general construction of "foliated" backgrounds for M-theory compactifications, building on the recently proposed geometric construction of M-theory compactifications on twisted compactifications of CY 3-folds. These backgrounds generalize the warped product construction, and provide a new class of examples for M-theory compactifications, with nontrivial topology and dynamics. The dynamics includes both higher-dimensional gravity and a U(1) gauge field, arising as the m=0 reducing gauge field of M-theory. We analyze the low energy effective actions for these theories, and show that they can be described by a single, nontrivial function of the radial variable only, for a large class of examples. We propose a generalization of the warped AdS_3 solution, where the warping function and the 3-form flux are functions of the U(1) gauge field. We show that this generalization is motivated by a desire to have a well-defined bulk stress tensor, and that for a large class of examples, the low energy effective action is independent of the 3-form flux.

Recent advances in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved significant performance improvements in medical image segmentation. However, these methods face challenges in calibration and out-of-distribution (OD) detection. Calibration refers to the phenomenon where CNNs produce inconsistent predictions for the same input, and OD detection refers to the ability of a model to generalize to new, unseen data distributions. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to improve calibration and OD detection in medical image segmentation with CNNs. We introduce a temperature-scaling mechanism that dynamically adjusts the temperature parameter for the softmax function during inference. By applying temperature scaling, we can control the diversity of the model's predictions and improve calibration.

Semantic image segmentation remains a challenging task, especially for pixel-level classification. Although recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance, segmentation models still struggle in segmenting objects with complex shapes and scenes with extreme appearances. In this paper, we present a novel approach to semantic segmentation that incorporates spatial convolutional random walks into a unified framework to explicitly model the spatial dependencies and address the aforementioned challenges. Our approach harnesses the power of graph neural networks to capture the intricate relationships between pixels, effectively leveraging the graphical representation of the input image. Specifically, we design a convolutional random walk layer that iteratively performs random walk computations on the feature tensors within a spatial-aware convolutional neural network architecture. This layer allows us to explicitly model the long-range dependencies in the image while retaining spatial coherence.

Rigid foam films are commonly used in the food industry as a packaging material due to their ability to provide insulation and reduce food waste. However, these films are known to have holes and cracks that can reduce their effectiveness. In this research, we use a combination of experimental and numerical methods to investigate the effect of holes and cracks on the thermal conductivity of rigid foam films. We find that the presence of holes and cracks can significantly reduce the thermal conductivity of the film, and that the reduction in thermal conductivity is dependent on the size and shape of the holes and cracks. We also find that the thermal conductivity of the film is inversely proportional to the thickness of the film. 

 Understanding the impact of holes and cracks on the thermal conductivity of rigid foam films is important for improving the performance of these materials as food packaging.

We present an efficient, fully-automated and interactive system for segmenting medical images through deep learning. Our system is based on fully convolutional neural networks (FCN), which enable efficient inference on entire slides with high throughput. Unlike existing FCN-based approaches, which rely on pre-defined network architectures and training protocols, we introduce an adaptive architecture that dynamically varies across tiles within each slide. This allows our system to achieve better segmentation performance by leveraging local information, and results in better utilization of computational resources during inference. We employ a tile-based processing paradigm that can effectively utilize modern GPU memory, and show that our method achieves real-time performance on slides with sizes up to 512^2 pixels. In a user study, we show that our interactive segmentation method achieves higher accuracy and faster performance compared to a state-of-the-art automated method.

Recent progress in segmentation of medical images typically relies on large amounts of annotated training data. However, different diseases might require different segmentation strategies due to distinct anatomical changes, and it can be difficult to obtain large-scale annotated data for all domains. We propose a framework to learn a disease-specific segmentation model for MRI brain images using only a small labeled sample of healthy and diseased images. Our framework is based on the observation that anatomical structures of the brain, as well as most diseases, manifest themselves in spatially coherent patterns, which can be captured by learned spatial filters. We propose to learn a shared low-dimensional embedding of brain images, where the embedding is optimized to (1) capture disease-specific spatial patterns and (2) be useful for segmentation. The embedding is learned via a conditional cycle consistency loss, which ensures that the embedding encodes spatial relationships both within and between images.

Recent works on semantic segmentation have achieved remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, but most lack the ability to generalize to unseen domains. In this paper, we investigate the use of generative models, namely Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), for producing more robust feature representations for semantic segmentation. We propose a semi-supervised approach where a GAN is trained to synthesize training samples in the target domain, and show that this leads to improved performance and robustness. To effectively utilize the limited labeled data in each target domain, we propose a novel consistency loss that enforces the segmentation model to be robust to variations in the unlabeled images, as well as a domain-adversarial loss that explicitly trains the model to recognize differences between domains. When tested on the Cityscapes dataset, our approach yields meaningful improvements in segmentation quality and out-of-domain robustness, even with no target-domain labels. We further demonstrate the generalization capability of our approach on two different datasets: a synthetic dataset rendered from a 3D city model and a real-world dataset captured by an autonomous driving car.

The effect of electron irradiation on the superconductivity in single crystals of Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Ru$_{x}$)$_2$As$_2$ ($x=$0.24) was investigated. The critical temperature was found to increase with electron irradiation dose. The critical temperature increases are attributed to the creation of additional charge carriers by the irradiation induced defects. The irradiation induced defects also reduce the superfluid density. The reduction of the superfluid density is more pronounced in the samples with higher irradiation doses. The results are compared with previous results on other iron-based superconductors.

Gaussian dynamic convolution (GDC) is a fast approximation of spatial convolution that exploits the locality and orientation of filters to achieve significant acceleration. However, existing GDC methods are not directly applicable to pixel-level segmentation, because they use a small number of fixed filters with limited expressive power. In this paper, we extend GDC to a new framework named Gaussian dynamic conditional random fields (GDC-CRF), which is capable of capturing complex local patterns for pixel-level segmentation. We construct a stack of Gaussian filters from a set of orientation-specific filters with distinct scales, and dynamically compute the response of the Gaussian filters according to the multi-scale orientation of the input features. Our framework is essentially a Gaussian dynamic convolution (GDC) that replaces the fixed filterbank with a set of Gaussian filters. We derive a closed-form solution for the GDC-CRF, and further simplify it into a linear solve by introducing a new sparse prior.

Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are indispensable for the diagnosis of cardiac abnormalities, but the process of manually annotating ECG waveforms is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Recently, deep learning models have been proposed for ECG delineation, but these models require a large amount of manually annotated data for training. In this work, we present ECG-DelNet, a deep learning model for ECG delineation that can be trained using a mixed quality dataset, containing both manually annotated and automatically annotated data. We show that our model can learn to delineate ECG waveforms with high accuracy, even when trained on a mixed quality dataset. Our model is composed of a convolutional neural network (CNN) followed by a region-based fully connected neural network (FNN). We evaluate our model on a large dataset of ambulatory ECGs and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art in ECG delineation.

We present a method for decomposing a 3D scene into objects via unsupervised volume segmentation. Our method is based on the observation that object surfaces exhibit a higher curvature than the background. We leverage this property to develop a curvature-based volume segmentation method. We compute a curvature potential directly in the voxel space using a Gauss-Newton technique for efficient non-differentiable structure and motion estimation. Furthermore, we propose an iterative refinement framework to optimize the segmentation. We evaluate our method on the ShapeNet part segmentation benchmark and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art on both the car and airplane categories.

We address the problem of multi-target tracking of asynchronous objects, as encountered in asynchronous video sequences analysis or multi-sensor surveillance. We propose to handle the corresponding measurement models as superpositional; i.e., we allow for multiple objects to be present in any given measurement. This modeling leads to a tractable, yet general, representation of measurements in terms of labeled random finite sets (RFS). We propose a particle filter that maintains an RFS representation of the state, and propose an efficient algorithm for predicting the evolution of the state RFS. The algorithm operates on the principle of forward filtering backward sampling, and is significantly faster than existing methods that operate on the principle of backward sampling forward filtering. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a real-world problem of airplane tracking in asynchronous radar sequences.

We perform an in-depth analysis of the evolution of the Twitter social network, the massive online social network servicing 330 million users, by analyzing the graph properties of its social graph from 2007 to 2014. In particular, we study the evolution of six graph properties: size, average degree, clustering, modularity, path length, and triangle abundance. These properties capture important aspects of the network’s structure such as the number of nodes and edges, the density and connectedness of the graph, and the community structure present in the network. By studying the time dependence of these properties, we aim to gain insights into the evolution of the Twitter social network and how it changes over time. Our analysis shows that the Twitter social network has grown significantly since it was launched in 2006, with a steady increase in the number of users and tweets over time. The average degree has also increased steadily, indicating that users are increasingly connecting with each other on the network.

In this paper a new algorithm is presented for clustering categorical data. This algorithm is an extension of the Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm for continuous vector data. In contrast to the FCM algorithm, which requires the specification of a single parameter defining the granularity of clustering, the new algorithm incorporates a degree of uncertainty, or fuzziness, in the specification of the cluster membership, making it more flexible and able to capture the inherent uncertainty in clustering. This algorithm has been developed to perform clustering on a new data type, referred to as vector membership (VM) data. VM data combines categorical and vector data in a single data representation. The proposed algorithm partitions VM data according to the belonging degrees of the constituent vectors to different clusters.

We study the pattern avoidance for set partitions, introducing a new forbidden family of patterns. Given a set system $\{S_1,\dots,S_m\}$, we say that a partition $P$ of $[m]$ avoids the $k$-way partition pattern if there is no set system $\{T_1,\dots,T_m\}$ such that each $T_i$ is a union of at most $k$ sets from $\{S_1,\dots,S_m\}$ and $P$ is isomorphic to the partition of $[m]$ induced by $\{T_1,\dots,T_m\}$. Pattern avoidance has been previously considered for set systems. In this setting, pattern avoidance was defined in terms of unions of consecutive sets in the given system. Our new forbidden family generalizes the patterns considered in the previous works, while keeping the parameter $k$ fixed. We study the pattern avoidance for set partitions `a la Klazar', introducing a new forbidden family of patterns. It is shown that, unlike the pattern avoidance for set systems, the pattern avoidance for set partitions is not monotone.

The work describes a three-fluid (air, water and particulate) simulation using a coupled set of fluid flow equations. The particulate phase is treated using the discrete element method (DEM), while air and water are simulated using the multiphase flow module of OpenFOAM, an open-source computational fluid dynamics (CFD) package. The three components are coupled using a drag force prescribed between the particulate phase and the fluid phases. The model is evaluated against experimental data obtained from a 0.1 m3/s air flow over a flat plate with water spray and spherical particles injection. Good agreement is observed between the model predictions and the experimental data for the air side pressure drop and velocity profile, water side pressure drop, water spray penetration and spherical particles trajectories and deposition. The predicted particulate phase velocity and distributions show good agreement with the measurements as well.

We study the topology of random graphs and, more generally, of fully connected random fields, in the large size limit. For instance, we show that the associated graph almost surely displays a giant component, which is characterized by an exponential number of nodes. We prove a structural result, according to which any two nodes in the giant component are almost surely connected by a chain of other nodes, each of which belongs to at most one of a certain number of ``Stochastic Cliques''. These cliques are sparse: each of them contains an exponential number of nodes, but their total number is only polynomial. We also show that any two nodes in the giant component are connected by a path, each of whose edges belongs to an expected proportion of at most $\frac{4}{\sqrt{n}}$ stochastic cliques. Our results are based on a particular coupling of the graphical representation of the random field, which we also use to define a natural generalization of the notion of triangle in the case of a multi-variate field.

Magnetic reconnection is a fundamental process in plasma physics, by which magnetic fields deconnect and merge, converting magnetic energy into other forms like particle heating. In this work, we investigate the effect of including large-scale effective potentials in the collisionless magnetic reconnection framework. We show that the large-scale dynamics modifies the particle distributions in the reconnection layer, affecting the ion heating. The effective potentials act as a converging lens that traps ions, modifying their trajectories. We observe that this trapping effect reduces the ion heating compared to the case without the large-scale dynamics. The reduction of ion heating is more significant when the strength of the effective potential is stronger.

Deep learning ensembles have shown promising results for medical image segmentation. However, they require large amounts of data and training time when training on small datasets. We propose a deep learning ensemble method, called deep ensembles based on Stochastic Activation Selection (S2EN), which trains ensemble networks with shared weights, each consisting of randomly selected activation functions from a pre-defined activation pool. Since the ensemble networks share weights and the selected activation functions act as regularization, the proposed method reduces the amount of training data and time needed to achieve high performance, making it suitable for training with small datasets. We applied the proposed method to polyp segmentation in colorectal endoscopic videos, and compared it with a recently proposed deep learning ensemble method as well as a state-of-the-art deep learning method based on a two-stream network. The proposed method achieved a 3.6% and 2.8% improvement in F1-score on the validation and test datasets, respectively, compared to the next best method.

Biofilms are dense microbial communities encapsulated in an extracellular matrix, which protects the cells from harsh environmental conditions and allows cells to enter dormancy. The microbial communities in biofilms are very different from planktonic cultures, which are suspended in liquid media. Microbial dormancy is a general term for the various strategies that microorganisms use to survive under adverse conditions. This thesis presents a novel model of microbial dormancy in biofilms and planktonic cultures, which could explain why some microorganisms remain dormant for long periods of time. This model could also help to understand how microorganisms in biofilms respond to environmental changes and how they recover from dormancy. 

 The data also suggest that some microorganisms may be able to switch between different states of dormancy, depending on the environmental conditions.

The Belle II pixel detector, which is one of the main detectors of the Belle II experiment, is designed to measure the positions and energies of the particles produced in the collision point of the $e^+e^-$ accelerator. It is a double-sided detector with silicon pixels and it is located immediately after the beam pipe at the collision point. The FPGA based data read-out system is designed to process the signals from the pixel detector and transmit the processed data to the computing system. The read-out system consists of custom logic boards and commercial FPGAs. The custom logic boards are responsible for the communication with the pixel detector and the transmission of the data to the FPGAs. The FPGAs are used to process the data and transmit it to the computing system.

We introduce Points2Polygons, an approach for training a geometric context-based segmentation model using only weak labels, i.e., point-level labels. Our model segments images based on the underlying geometric context of the weak labels. We introduce an encoder-decoder architecture that leverages the geometric consistency of object segments to refine initial predictions. We train our model using an adversarial loss that encourages the model to produce segmentations with geometric properties similar to the weak labels. Our method does not require any post-processing steps, such as graph cuts or conditional random fields. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and KITTI datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the weakly-supervised segmentation task.

We present a method for segmenting images based on the content of screens present in the image. Our method comprises two stages: in the first stage we identify regions in the image that contain screens, and in the second stage we segment the content displayed on those screens. Our proposed method is fully automatic, and is able to handle a variety of screen content, including text, images, and videos. We evaluate our method on a new dataset we created, as well as on publicly available datasets, and show that it performs better than state-of-the-art methods.

 Our screen content segmentation algorithm proceeds by modeling the image as a sparse combination of dictionary elements, where each dictionary element corresponds to a candidate screen content patch. We simultaneously identify regions containing screens, and segment the content on the screens by selecting the appropriate dictionary elements.

Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely relies on large-scale labeled datasets, which are expensive to collect and annotate. When training a segmentation model, the distribution of the labeled source domain might be significantly different from that of the target domain, where the model will be deployed. To overcome this domain shift, we propose a source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) approach for image segmentation, which requires no labeled source data. Specifically, we learn a joint distribution of appearance and geometry for the target domain to adapt the pre-trained model for segmentation. We propose to minimize the divergence between the estimated joint distribution and the product of the estimated appearance and geometry distributions for consistency. Furthermore, to effectively estimate the distributions, we propose to maximize the correlation between their estimates and the ground truth labels.

Semantic image segmentation is crucial for understanding the content of an image, and it remains a challenging task. One reason is the diversity of visual instances in the real world. For example, accurately segmenting objects with complex shapes or textures can be difficult. We present a novel locally adaptive learning loss (LALL) for semantic image segmentation, which adaptively reweights the learning process according to the local characteristics of each pixel. The proposed method captures the underlying structure of the data by modeling the spatial dependence of pixel labels, and it can be integrated into any deep learning framework. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LALL on semantic image segmentation, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset with only a small number of training samples.

We present a novel semi-supervised learning (SSL) approach to address the 2D medical image segmentation problem. The proposed method utilizes a contrastive learning strategy, which maximizes the similarity between the labeled and unlabeled data, and minimizes the similarity between different unlabeled data samples. To achieve this, we adopt a supervised clustering algorithm that utilizes a labeled data pool to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled data. We optimize the clustering algorithm parameters to minimize the contrastive loss, which measures the similarity between the labeled and unlabeled data, and the cross-entropy loss, which measures the similarity between different unlabeled data. Furthermore, we introduce a data augmentation technique that generates additional training samples by applying geometric transformations to the original data. The proposed method is evaluated on the 2D abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) segmentation benchmark from the 2018 Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) challenge.

We present a simple yet effective approach for instance-based object detection and recognition. Our method performs object detection and recognition by detecting objects with a priority on the instance level. We employ an object detection framework based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) for prominent object detection and recognition. The proposed method focuses on the detection of whole objects with high recall and low precision. Then, the detected objects are recognized by a modified CNN that is trained to recognize the detected objects with a priority on the instance level. We evaluate our method on the VOC 2007 dataset and compare it to other state-of-the-art object detection and recognition methods.

We present a novel end-to-end differentiable decomposition framework for training convolutional neural network (CNN) based conditional random fields (CRFs). Under this framework, the CNN-CRF is decomposed into a convolutional layer and a CRF layer, with the convolutional layer outputting particle filters for the CRF layer. The particle filters are obtained by solving a convolutional-deconvolutional (c-d) network via a differentiable approximation. During training, the gradients of the CNN-CRF with respect to the CRF layer and the convolutional layer are calculated via the chain rule and the backpropagation algorithm. Our framework is capable of effectively training deep CNN-CRFs with multiple layers. We validate our framework on a number of benchmark datasets, and demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency.

Recent results on image segmentation could be improved both in accuracy and efficiency, especially when only a small amount of labeled data is available. In this paper, we exploit self-correcting networks (SCN) to boost the performance of semantic image segmentation. We train SCNs in an semi-supervised learning setting, where a small amount of labeled data is available for training, and exploit a large amount of unlabeled data to implicitly learn to correct the segmentation errors. Specifically, we train two SCNs, one produces segmentation maps with only pixel-level supervision, and the other produces segmentation maps by refining the former with image-level supervision. We show that the latter can be effectively trained with only unlabeled data. In the experimental part, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on the PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark.

We present a novel approach for enhancing 3D morphological feature representation in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for semantic segmentation of medical images. Our method involves extracting 3D morphological features from medical images using morphological operations, which are then used as input to a CNN. We propose a new block design, called the residual block, which enhances the representation of the extracted features by learning residual mappings. The proposed residual block is designed to mitigate the information loss caused by linear transformations in traditional convolutional layers, such as downsampling and normalization. We evaluate our method on the task of semantic segmentation of abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance. Our code and dataset are publicly available.

Recent progresses in convolutional neural network (CNN) elevate image-to-image (I2I) translation to a new horizon, but most existing methods require a large amount of labeled source images for training, which is difficult to obtain in many real-world applications. In this paper, we attempt to address this issue by introducing a new I2I translation framework with extremely weak supervision, where only a few labeled source images and a large number of unlabeled source images are available for training. In particular, we first train a teacher network with a few labeled source images to obtain pseudo labels for all source images. Then, we learn a student network with the pseudo labels and the unlabeled source images for I2I translation. To further improve the translation quality, we present a cycle-consistent loss to enhance the learning of the student network. Finally, we evaluate our method on the Cityscapes dataset for urban scene understanding, and experimental results show the effectiveness of our method.

We introduce set-valued fundamental diagrams for second-order traffic models. Set-valued fundamental diagrams extend classical fundamental diagrams, which are known to be applicable only for bottleneck flows and strictly saturated traffic. Set-valued diagrams can explicitly account for the possibility of having a set of possible output flows for a given input flow. These diagrams are derived from Jaminon solutions, which are characterized via the second-order limit of generalized bottleneck equations. In this paper, we construct the set-valued fundamental diagrams for several classes of networks, including series-parallel and tree networks. The results show that the constructed set-valued diagrams are closely related to the generalized Bottleneck Principles and the generalized network decomposition.

Recent progress in deep learning has enabled the development of effective models for remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation. However, these models often suffer from boundary loss, which can lead to inaccurate results and hinder their performance in real-world applications. In this paper, we investigate the boundary loss problem and propose a novel approach to address it. Our approach consists of a boundary-aware loss function that explicitly considers the boundary regions during training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two public remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation benchmarks, and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Our code and model weights are publicly available.

In this paper, we present an effective cloud detection and segmentation algorithm for satellite imagery based on a gradient-based approach. Our algorithm utilizes the gradient information of the input image to detect and segment clouds, and is capable of handling both bright and dark clouds. We apply our algorithm to the PERSIANN-CCS dataset, which consists of satellite images labeled with ground truth information, and evaluate its performance against the current state-of-the-art method. Our results show that our algorithm significantly improves the cloud detection and segmentation performance, resulting in an F1-score of 0.8519 and a precision of 0.8279.

 Our algorithm consists of three main steps: gradient computation, gradient-based filtering, and post-processing. The gradient computation step calculates the gradient information of the input image, which is then used in the gradient-based filtering step to detect and segment clouds.

We present a method for the semantic segmentation of video sequences using convolutional LSTM networks. Our approach employs a hybrid convolutional and recurrent architecture that models both appearance and motion dynamics over time. We introduce a novel temporal max-pooling layer, which enables the network to selectively focus on the most relevant information while being invariant to input order. Our method naturally handles variable-length inputs and is applicable to arbitrary video durations. We evaluate our approach on the CamVid dataset and show that our model outperforms the state of the art in semantic video segmentation.

  Our approach to semantic segmentation of video sequences is based on a hybrid convolutional and recurrent architecture that models both appearance and motion dynamics over time.

Recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation. However, these models usually demand a large amount of labeled data for superior performance, which is difficult to obtain in the medical field. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel multi-scale self-guided attention (MSA) module to enhance the performance of medical image segmentation models. Our approach combines a multi-scale attention module and a self-guided attention module to capture the global and local features respectively. The multi-scale attention module can capture the global context by aggregating the features at multiple scales, while the self-guided attention module can focus on the important regions by learning a weighting function. We evaluate our approach on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, and our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

RatLesNetv2 is a fully-convolutional network for segmenting rat brain lesions in MRI scans. It employs an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling module to capture multi-scale context and a weighted loss function to address class imbalance. The network was trained on a large dataset of over 4000 images from 94 rats and evaluated on a separate test set. Compared to the previously published RatLesNet, RatLesNetv2 achieved higher accuracy and improved reproducibility. Further, RatLesNetv2 defines a new state-of-the-art for rodent brain lesion segmentation, outperforming other methods in terms of both F1-score and recall. The network is implemented using the PyTorch deep learning framework and is available at https://github.com/RatLesNet/RatLesNet.

Recent progress in medical image segmentation has largely been achieved by pre-training large models on large-scale, open-domain datasets, and then fine-tuning on in-domain data. However, fine-tuning tends to cause model capacity reduction and suffers from the lack of available in-domain training data. In this paper, we attempt to address both issues. We propose a Margin Preserving Self-paced Contrastive Learning (MPSCL) framework for unsupervised domain adaptation of medical image segmentation. Specifically, we use a margin-preserving learning scheme to alleviate the capacity reduction of the fine-tuning process, and a self-paced learning strategy, which allows the model to select the most informative data samples for adaptation, to address the data scarcity problem. We apply the proposed method to adapt a pre-trained model from abdominal CT to abdominal MRI segmentation with promising results.

We introduce a technique for class-independent full image segmentation, using a convolutional neural network. Our method is driven by a novel architecture, termed attention-within-segment, that is trained in an end-to-end manner on pixel-level ground truth data. In a single forward pass, our network outputs a segmentation mask for the entire image. A key distinction of our approach is that each pixel in the segmentation mask is assigned a "hard" segmentation class (e.g., object or background) or a "soft" attention weight, with the latter indicating the likelihood that a pixel belongs to a particular object. During inference, the soft attention weights are thresholded using a heuristic method based on a statistical test to obtain a final segmentation. To handle class-imbalanced datasets, we propose an extension of the attention-within-segment architecture that incorporates a loss-balancing term in the objective function.

In this paper, we present an approach for the segmentation of microscopy data for the purpose of identifying and locating nuclei in breast tissue images. We utilize a combination of techniques including image enhancement, thresholding, and morphological operations as preprocessing steps, with the primary segmentation approach utilizing a variant of the watershed transform. The watershed transform, initialized using gradient vector flow, is applied to the enhanced image, and then refined using a gradient-based approach. The resulting segmentation is evaluated using both manual and automated measures. The automated measure utilizes a graph cut based approach to evaluate the segmentation in a similar manner to the ground truth annotation. Results of the segmentation are presented, as are comparisons to other approaches.

Abstract: Cloud computing is a emerging technology that offers an array of advantages such as cost efficiency, scalability, and accessibility. However, it also raises security concerns, especially in the area of file management. This paper surveys the security issues in file management in cloud computing environment. It discusses the different security threats and vulnerabilities that exist in cloud computing and how they can impact file management. It also explores the various security measures and solutions that can be employed to mitigate these risks. The survey includes a comprehensive analysis of the existing research and literature on the subject.

Recent works on semantic segmentation largely focus on designing models with better expressive power to leverage abundant annotated image data for training. However, these models are known to be susceptible to the inherent ambiguity of pixel-level annotations, and their complexity can make them difficult to optimize. In this paper, we take a different approach and treat energy learning as a combinatorial problem, where the goal is to design an energy function that can effectively encode segmentations for a specific task. Our key observation is that when the energy function is a composition of simple parts, the search for a good segmentation can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem, for which efficient algorithms exist. To learn a good composition of parts, we propose a novel framework called Combinatorial Energy Learning (CEL). Given a database of image segmentations, CEL learns a segmentation energy function as a weighted composition of a set of predefined atomic energies, where the weights are optimized via combinatorial optimization.

Recent developments in MRI acquisition enable the acquisition of multiple contrasts confounding the manual delineation of the thalamus. We propose a method to segment the thalamus in MRI volumes acquired with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and magnetization transfer (MT) weighted imaging. Our approach is based on a multi-atlas segmentation framework leveraging the structural and the functional information available in those two contrasts. We used 50 manually annotated atlases built from synthetic brains generated with Diffusion Toolkit (DITK), and two atlases built from real MRI datasets to obtain an initial segmentation of the thalamus. Then, to combine the information provided by the atlases, we defined a cost function that quantifies the disagreement between the predicted segmentations and the ground truth labels in the atlases. We used a greedy algorithm to obtain the final segmentation where the cost is minimized.

The Third Gravitational Lensing Accuracy Testing (GREAT3) Challenge Handbook summarizes the ongoing work of the GREAT3 collaboration, which is performing a rigorous test of gravitational lensing as a tool for astrophysical measurement. The collaboration compares measurements of the same gravitational lens made by many different research groups, to evaluate the systematics and uncertainties in the measurements. This comparison is done in a blind fashion, so that evaluators do not know which group took which measurement when performing the comparison. This challenge has run twice before, in 2004 and 2009, and has spurred significant improvements in lensing measurement techniques. We present the protocols for the third challenge, as well as an overview of the current state of the field. A summary of the current state of the challenge is also provided.

Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely relies on large-scale training data with ground truth segmentations. Creating pixel-level annotations for a large number of images is expensive and requires expert knowledge. As a consequence, only a limited number of images is annotated, leading to an imbalance in training data: most images have no direct pixel-level annotations. In this paper, we study the problem of identifying reliable segmentations from a large number of noisy and incomplete annotators. We present a new method to identify the most reliable annotators for a given image and use their annotations to improve the performance of a segmentation model. We propose a new differentiable scoring function that is optimized end-to-end with a segmentation model.

We develop a stochastic Eulerian-Lagrangian method for simulating fluid-structure interactions with thermal fluctuations. The fluid domain is discretized on a fixed Eulerian grid, while the structure is modeled as a set of discrete Lagrangian particles. The fluid flow is governed by the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, which are solved using a stochastic finite element method. The solid particles are treated as tracers in the fluid domain and are updated using a Lagrangian scheme. The interaction between the fluid and the structure is achieved through a no-slip boundary condition on the surface of the particles and a drag force that acts on the particles due to the fluid flow. The thermal fluctuations are introduced through a stochastic heat flux in the wall region of the fluid domain.

We introduce the notion of certified self-stabilization, where the assurance that a distributed system is stabilizing is formalized and proven correct using the Coq system. As a case study, we provide a certified self-stabilizing implementation of the popular dining philosophers protocol. The key technical challenges in the development of a framework for certified self-stabilization involve formalizing the notion of a stabilizing system and proving relevant theorems, e.g., if a system satisfies certain properties, then it is stabilizing. Since stability is a temporal concept, modeling and proving stability properties, in general, require techniques for reasoning about infinite state spaces. To overcome this difficulty, the framework formalizes stability using only finite-state models, by expressing stability in terms of a finite-state abstraction. The key components of the abstraction are (1) an asynchronous finite-state machine (AFSM) that captures the finite-state behavior of the system, and (2) a finite-state overlay that captures the infinite-state behavior of the system in a compact way.

We introduce a simple and effective image segmentation approach called Super-BPD (Super Boundary-to-Pixel Direction), which achieves fast and almost linear runtime. Given an image, our method first estimates pixel-level labels by a super-resolution network, and then predicts boundary-to-pixel direction (BPD) fields from the estimated labels. The BPD fields are formulated as a sparse coding problem, which can be efficiently solved by modern optimization methods. During the segmentation, we only need to perform a few iterations (less than 10) to achieve the results with promising quality. Our approach is trained in a self-supervised manner, and able to run at almost linear speed, thus it is suitable for large-scale images. In the experiment, we test our method on two public available datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach against other state-of-the-art segmentation approaches.

We develop a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) radiative transfer code for calculating spectral line formation in cool stars. The code consists of an improved version of the 1D LTE stellar spectral synthesis code of Werner [CITE] for calculating the level populations of 24 chemical elements, and a newly developed LTE-to-NLTE spectral synthesis code that calculates the NLTE spectral line profiles based on the level population obtained from the stellar spectral synthesis code. We have calculated the NLTE spectral line profiles for several elements in the wavelength range between 1000 Å and 1 μm, and found that the NLTE effects can be very important, especially for the weak lines. The abundance derived from the weak lines can be different from the LTE abundance by 0.5 dex or more. We have also found that the derived abundance of some elements, such as Ca, Cr, Mn, and Ni, depends on the choice of the model atmosphere, and the line lists used in the calculations.

We present a method for automated segmentation of retinal layers from optical coherence tomography (OCT) images using geodesic distance. OCT images are acquired using an optical coherence tomography system, and the retinal layers are segmented using a graph-based segmentation algorithm. The graph is constructed by computing the geodesic distance between a set of seed points and the OCT image data. The geodesic distance is computed using a fast marching algorithm, which iteratively updates the distance from the seed points to the OCT image data. The resulting graph represents the connectivity between the seed points and the OCT image data, and can be used to segment the retinal layers. The performance of the algorithm was evaluated on a dataset of OCT images, and the results show that the algorithm is able to accurately segment the retinal layers.

We perform the first systematic study of the oscillations in solar jets observed with the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) of the Hinode mission. We have identified oscillating structures in 26 jets during 2007-2009, mainly in the chromosphere, but also in the transition region and in the corona. These oscillations are likely to be driven by the reconnection process in coronal loops. We have characterized the oscillations using time-distance diagrams, and measured the proper motions of several hundreds of oscillating points. These measurements allow us to investigate, for the first time, the spatial dependence of the oscillation period in a jet, with the period increasing with height. We have also found that the oscillations are likely to be radially propagating away from the jet axis with a propagation speed of about 20 km/s in the chromosphere, and 40 km/s in the transition region.

Recent work has shown that the human brain uses probabilistic body schema representations to plan and execute reaching movements in everyday life. These internal representations are inferred from incoming sensory information and guide the online selection of the most probable limb pose. Here we investigate the role of tactile feedback in the online estimation of body schema during aiming movements of the arm. In a virtual reality experiment, participants executed random reaching movements towards target locations with their right arm, while their left arm was immobilized. During the movements, we abruptly switched off the visual feedback and the participants had to rely on somatosensory feedback for continuing the movement. We find that the robustness of continuation after the visual interruption increases with the number of reached targets during the movement, indicating a learning effect.

Abstract
This paper presents an automated pavement crack segmentation approach using a U-Net-based convolutional neural network (CNN). The U-Net architecture, developed for biomedical image processing, is adapted to pavement crack image segmentation. The proposed method consists of three steps: image acquisition, preprocessing, and crack segmentation using a U-Net-based CNN. In the image acquisition step, pavement images are collected using a vehicle-mounted mobile device. In the preprocessing step, the images are preprocessed to enhance the contrast and reduce noise. In the segmentation step, the U-Net-based CNN is utilized to automatically segment the pavement cracks.

Semantic image segmentation has gained increasing attention, as it alleviates the manual effort required for pixel-level labeling by automatically assigning a class label to each pixel in an image. Most existing works focus on accurately classifying pixels within the interior of objects, while the boundary pixels are often treated as a derivative of the interior pixels, resulting in suboptimal performance around object boundaries. In this paper, we argue that the boundary regions carry significant information that can be exploited to improve the segmentation performance. To this end, we propose a novel approach called Boundary-informed Classification (Boa), which explicitly models the boundary regions to capture the additional information. Boa first detects boundary pixels using a simple yet effective boundary detector, and then utilizes a boundary-informed loss function to enhance the classification of boundary pixels during training. In the inference stage, we develop an adaptive inference mechanism that can effectively utilize the boundary information for accurate segmentation.

Recent works have shown that training vision transformers (ViTs) with millions of parameters can outperform their convolutional neural network (CNN) counterparts on image classification tasks. However, training ViTs still poses several challenges: models are sensitive to (1) the quality and amount of data, (2) the augmentation strategies, and (3) the regularization techniques. In this work, we investigate how these components impact the performance and generalization of ViTs. We find that training ViTs with higher quality data improves performance significantly, and larger models require more data to maintain performance. We show that the right augmentation strategy can boost the performance of a ViT, particularly when the amount of data is not sufficient. We further explore several regularization techniques and demonstrate their effectiveness in improving generalization.

Recent works have shown that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) benefit 3D biomedical image segmentation, alleviating the shortcomings of conventional fully convolutional networks (FCNs). Nonetheless, training end-to-end architectures that combine FCNs and RNNs is challenging due to the non-differentiability of slice-wise max pooling. In this work, we propose a novel architecture that combines FCNs and RNNs, termed Recurrent Fully Convolutional Network (RFCN), which is trained end-to-end. We overcome the non-differentiability issue by using a differentiable pooling technique. We assess the proposed architecture on the challenging task of myocardial segmentation in cardiac MR images. Our method achieves a competitive performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods, without any pre-processing steps such as initializing the network with a pre-trained FCN.

Timed tree automata extend tree automata with timers that model the evolution of system behaviors. Existing techniques for checking safety properties of timed systems often reduce the analysis of timed automata to untimed automata, which discard the information about timing constraints in the original system model. This can result in losing the timing information in the final verification results. We present a new technique for checking safety properties of timed systems using timed tree automata. Our technique explicitly takes into account the timing information in the system model, and provides a fine-grained analysis that reveals the timing behavior of the system. We have implemented our technique in the Timed Tree Automata Checker, which is available as open-source software.

We present a technique for the forward and backward propagation of convolutional neural networks that is optimized for pixelwise classification tasks. Our method achieves a significant speedup compared to standard techniques, with a negligible reduction in accuracy. We present results showing that our method can speed up the training process by as much as a factor of two, with no loss in accuracy. We also show that our method can be used to improve the performance of existing convolutional neural networks, resulting in a significant increase in accuracy with only a small increase in training time. Our method is based on a simple yet effective technique for optimizing the forward and backward propagation of convolutional neural networks. We believe that our method will be useful for many applications, including the training of large-scale convolutional neural networks.

Traditional fuzzy C-means (FCM) clustering algorithms suffer from the occurrence of local minima in iterative optimization of the objective function during the clustering process. We propose a kernelized weighted SUSAN based FCM clustering algorithm to segment images affected by Gaussian noise. Noisy images degrade the quality of feature vectors for traditional FCM algorithms that are extracted from the original images. In the proposed algorithm, a kernelization technique is employed during the feature extraction to mitigate the effects of noise. Then, to further improve the quality of feature vectors, a weighted strategy is introduced where the weights are determined by using the SUSAN (symmetric unambiguous structures and anomalies) test. The SUSAN based weights can effectively reduce the influence of outliers in the feature vectors.

Semantic segmentation of high-resolution satellite imagery is a fundamental task for extracting useful information. However, the severe variation of scales in the same scene poses a great challenge for pixel-level labeling. In this paper, we propose a new approach for semantic segmentation of high-resolution satellite imagery, named PP-LinkNet. It leverages a multi-stage training strategy to learn the hierarchical representations of pixels, which can effectively capture both local and global characteristics of the data. Specifically, a pyramid pooling module is proposed to encode multi-scale contextual information, and a link-net module is designed to capture the global relationships between pixels. The whole network is trained in an end-to-end manner, allowing effective gradient flow through the pyramid and link structures.

Recent progress in interactive segmentation has primarily focused on extracting object boundaries accurately rather than the entire object region. While boundary-based methods can achieve better performance, they often require a time-consuming initial segmentation step to generate the boundary predictions. Moreover, interactions for these methods become complicated as they involve modifying the boundary rather than the entire object region. In this paper, we present EdgeFlow, a framework for achieving practical interactive segmentation with edge-guided flow. It leverages a boundary-based approach but removes the initial segmentation step, making the interaction process as intuitive as the recent region-based methods. Specifically, given a preliminary segmentation result, EdgeFlow directly optimizes the segmentation by introducing a novel edge-guided flow, which can effectively propagate the user's modifications to the entire object region while maintaining the boundary details.

We present LooseCut, a novel interactive segmentation method that leverages loosely bounded boxes for initializing and refining segmentation results. Our method improves upon the state-of-the-art in two ways. First, we propose a new relaxed bounding box formulation, which affords a larger margin for error in the initial bounding box placement while preserving the ability to capture the object of interest. Second, we propose an iterative refinement process that utilizes geometric constraints to reduce the prediction error, allowing for improved segmentation results. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark while being faster than all other interactive methods. In addition, through an user study, we show that our method is preferred by users compared to the baseline and other interactive methods in terms of speed and usability.

We address the problem of modeling physical forces in active contours for image segmentation, using a locally-varying curvature approximation. This model can simulate a priori unknown forces, derived from the image itself, which drive the active contour toward a segmentation. The energy of the proposed active contour model is minimized by a fast marching method, which iteratively updates the contour. This approach yields a fast and efficient algorithm, which is very competitive, in terms of computational speed, with traditional active contour models based on gradient descent. In addition, a priori knowledge about the forces, such as upper and lower bounds, further accelerates the algorithm and leads to a parameter-free method. The proposed method is applied to several images, and very promising results are obtained.

The British university sector has been at the forefront of web development and delivery of online information and services from the early days of the World Wide Web. The aim of the project described in this paper is to map the UK webspace by automatically analysing the contents of the websites of UK universities, in order to identify trends over time, and to provide a definitive record of the development of web provision and online services within UK Higher Education. In this paper we describe the initial findings from an analysis of the web spaces of UK universities over a period of three years, from 2004 to 2006. The analysis reveals a rapid growth in the size of web spaces, increasing from around 520 million pages in 2004 to over 1.1 billion pages in 2006. Over the same period the level of accessible content increased significantly, from around 820 million pages in 2004 to over 970 million pages in 2006. The number of websites hosted also increased substantially, from around 26,000 in 2004 to over 41,000 in 2006.
