A complex network and statistical mechanics approach

Introduction— Wikipedia is a multilingual online encyclopedia with editions maintained by registered volunteers, known as editors. It has become a popular resource for obtaining information, and its articles are widely used in search engines. However, the quality of articles varies widely, and the accuracy of information is variable. Users can modify articles directly, and it is estimated that there are more than 100,000 active contributors to Wikipedia. Editing of articles is generally collaborative and conversational, with editors expressing opinions and discussing changes.

We present an efficient graph cuts based technique for segmenting kidneys in ultrasound (US) images. Graph cuts methods have been widely used in image processing and computer vision for image segmentation. However, most existing methods rely on the initial segmentation results to obtain the final segmentation. In this work, we develop an adaptive graph cuts technique that can simultaneously consider the global and local features of the kidneys in US images. It can be used for the initial segmentation or as a stand-alone technique. Furthermore, we integrate multiple feature maps, including edge, regional, and texture information, into the graph cuts framework to achieve more accurate segmentation results.

Current state-of-the-art self-supervised semantic segmentation methods achieve impressive performance, but they rely on large amounts of manually designed architectural components and their hyperparameters. In this paper, we approach the problem of self-supervised semantic segmentation from a different angle. We propose a mix-and-match approach where we assemble a semantic segmentation network by combining off-the-shelf components from a large repository of pre-trained models, specifically tailoring our approach to the self-supervised setting. To this end, we introduce a new training regime for self-supervised segmentation, where we replace the normalisation layers of the segmentation network with random normalisation layers. This removes the need for manual tuning of many components, as well as allowing us to use segmentation networks as a black-box that is trained without accessing the internal representations. We evaluate our approach on ACDC and Cityscapes and show that our approach is able to achieve results that are competitive with the state-of-the-art, while requiring less manual design effort.

Vessel-CAPTCHA: An Efficient Learning Framework for Vessel Annotation and Segmentation. In this paper, we present a learning framework, namely Vessel-CAPTCHA, for the fully automatic vessel annotation and segmentation in 3D rotational angiography (3DRA) sequences. Unlike most existing methods which rely on handcrafted features, our approach learns a deep neural network to extract features directly from the raw input images. The network is composed of several convolutional layers with pooling operations, followed by fully connected layers for classification. To cope with the scarcity of annotated training samples, we adopt a bootstrapping strategy to train the network in an unsupervised manner, which is named as Vessel-CAPTCHA. In this approach, a vesselness measure is learned to select the regions of interest (ROIs) that are likely to be vessels, and these ROIs are then used to train a second network for the final vessel segmentation.

In this paper, we present a novel method for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MR images using a fully convolutional network. Our network is designed to take advantage of the hierarchical structure of the cardiac MR images, and it is composed of multiple stages of convolutional layers. We utilize a combination of atrous and regular convolutions to capture both local and global features in the images. Furthermore, we introduce a new loss function that combines the Dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to optimize the network for accurate segmentation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MICCAI 2012 cardiac segmentation challenge dataset, and it is able to segment the left ventricle with an accuracy of 97.6%.

 Our network architecture consists of multiple stages of convolutional layers, with each stage followed by a max-pooling layer.

Color image segmentation is the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments, each of which corresponds to a set of pixels sharing a common property. It has numerous applications in various fields of science and engineering including image processing, computer vision, and pattern recognition. Image enhancement, on the other hand, refers to the process of improving the quality of an image by increasing its contrast, brightness, or other visual properties. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study on the importance of image enhancement techniques in color image segmentation. We compare the performance of various image enhancement techniques, including histogram equalization, contrast stretching, and adaptive filtering, on a set of color images and evaluate their impact on the subsequent color image segmentation process. Our results show that image enhancement techniques have a significant impact on the accuracy and efficiency of color image segmentation and can greatly improve the overall performance of the segmentation process.

We present a multi-layer approach to superpixel-based higher-order conditional random field (CRF) for semantic image segmentation. In this approach, we first apply a simple yet effective superpixel segmentation method to extract a set of superpixels from the input image. Then, we construct a higher-order CRF model based on the extracted superpixels, where each superpixel is treated as a variable node and the semantic labels of the superpixels are treated as the hidden variables. The higher-order CRF model is learned in a supervised manner, where the semantic labels of the superpixels are predicted based on the appearance and the context information of the superpixels. The proposed approach is evaluated on the semantic image segmentation benchmark datasets of PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes. Experiment results show that the proposed approach achieves competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

We present an algorithm for maximin affinity learning of image segmentation. It is a hard assignment problem of learning a discrete labeling of a finite set of pixels given a finite set of labeled examples, with a penalty for labeling pixels differently from neighbors. Our algorithm is based on a novel approximation of the maximin criterion that enables the use of a gradient descent procedure with a convergence guarantee. We show that the algorithm is efficient in terms of both time and space, and we demonstrate its performance on a number of benchmark images.

 Introduction

The problem of assigning labels to pixels in images arises in many applications including image segmentation, texture analysis, and image registration. A wide range of techniques have been proposed for this problem.

Kernel spectral clustering (KSC) is a nonlinear dimension reduction technique and a general framework for clustering, pioneered by Davis et al. (2004). It encompasses several other kernel-based methods, such as kernel PCA and kernel Fisher discriminant analysis (Kernel-FDD), as special cases. This article provides a comprehensive introduction to KSC, covering the basic algorithm, theoretical properties, and practical tips for implementation. We also discuss extensions of KSC, including kernel CCA and kernel MDS, and applications in text mining, image analysis, and bioinformatics.

 Introduction

Spectral clustering is a popular technique for clustering and dimension reduction, originating from the spectral decomposition of symmetric positive semidefinite matrices. It has been shown to be effective in a variety of applications, including image analysis, text mining, and bioinformatics.

Recent works in visual object recognition typically operate on fixed sets of predefined objects or entities of interest. In this work, we introduce a new task of open-world entity segmentation, where the set of entities is not predefined but is rather determined by the data itself. We present an approach for open-world entity segmentation that discovers entities in an unsupervised manner, followed by an iterative refinement process that learns to localize and segment them. The unsupervised entity discovery is based on a variation of the non-parametric Dirichlet process, while the iterative refinement process is solved as a constrained optimization problem. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of instance-level segmentation of 40 different entity classes in the OpenWorld dataset, which contains over 100,000 images and requires zero-shot instance segmentation. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark.

Semidefinite programs (SDPs) appear in various applications, but they are challenging to solve when the dimensions are high. One reason for this is that SDPs require inverting matrices in order to compute the KKT conditions, and this operation can become computationally expensive when the dimension is large. In this paper, we propose a new method for reducing the dimension of SDPs using Jordan algebras. We show that the dimension of an SDP can be reduced via Jordan algebra techniques, and we provide a condition for when this reduction is possible. We implement our method in MATLAB and compare its performance to existing dimension reduction techniques. Our results show that our method can significantly improve the computational efficiency of SDPs, and it is particularly useful for problems with high dimensions.

We study a planar four-Fermi model in a tilted magnetic field using the functional renormalization group (FRG). We find a chiral phase transition line in the plane of the tilt angle and the coupling constant of the four-Fermi term. The chiral phase transition is of second order along the entire line. There is a critical point at a tilt angle of 45$^{\circ}$, where the correlation length exponent $\nu$ changes its value from 1 to 2. Along the line, the universality class is identical to that of the three-dimensional Ising model.

 We also analyze the FRG equations for the tilted axial next-nearest-neighbor Ising model in order to understand the appearance of the Ising universality class in the four-Fermi model.

In this paper, we study the problem of region homogeneity from a mathematical perspective. We propose a new definition of region homogeneity based on the concept of logarithmic image processing. Our definition is motivated by the observation that the logarithm of a pixel intensity value is a more robust representation of the pixel value in the presence of noise and interference. This leads to a new framework for image processing based on logarithmic image spaces. We show that the problem of region homogeneity can be formulated as a optimization problem in this new framework. We propose an algorithm to solve the optimization problem and show that the solution is a continuous function of the input image.

We study collective spontaneous emission from a system of quantum dots which are electrically controlled in a one-dimensional array. The quantum dots are described by the multi-mode Hartree-Fock theory, including the quantum defect, and the array is embedded in a photonic crystal. By calculating the emission spectrum and the electric field distribution, we show the existence of the hybrid light-matter states, which are formed by the strong coupling between the quantum dots and the photonic crystal cavity. The hybrid states show anti-crossing behavior with the uncoupled states of the quantum dots and the photonic crystal cavity. By means of the renormalization group technique, we investigate the quantum phase transition between the normal and the superradiant phases, and determine the critical number of quantum dots for the transition. The critical parameters are sensitive to both the quantum defects and the coupling between the dots and the photonic crystal.

We present a novel approach for ultra-high resolution image segmentation based on a locality-aware contextual correlation (LACC) model. Our approach exploits the contextual information of the image via a correlation prior, which captures the dependence between pixels belonging to the same object. To efficiently compute the correlation prior, we introduce a locality constraint that encourages similarity between pixels within a localized region. The LACC model is learned in a fully unsupervised manner via a variant of the expectation-maximization algorithm that optimizes the trade-off between the correlation prior and the locality prior. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the semantic segmentation of very high resolution remote sensing images, where the fine spatial granularity of the objects poses a challenge for most existing techniques. When compared to other state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods, our approach achieves superior performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

We introduce a general method for evaluating transport properties of disordered systems using microscopic simulations. This method is applicable to systems with both topological and thermal disorders, and it can be used to study a wide range of transport properties, including the conductivity, resistivity, and thermal conductivity. We begin by constructing an effective Hamiltonian for the disordered system, which captures the essential features of the disorder. This effective Hamiltonian is then used to calculate the quantum mechanical Green's function of the system, which in turn is used to compute the desired transport properties. The key advantage of this method is that it enables the calculation of transport properties with far fewer simulations than conventional methods, making it feasible to study systems with a large number of degrees of freedom.

 We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a number of different systems, including a model for disordered metals and a system with both topological and thermal disorders.

Recent advances in deep learning have achieved significant performance improvements for medical image segmentation. However, most of these approaches require large amounts of interactive labeling effort, which is expensive and time-consuming, and often impractical in clinical environments. In this paper, we present MIDeepSeg, a semi-supervised segmentation approach that minimizes the amount of interactive labeling effort required for training. Instead of using a fixed amount of labeled and unlabeled data, we iteratively add labeled data to the training set during training, which we call “minimally interactive” labeling. Our approach uses a simple yet effective deep learning architecture, and can be used to segment unseen objects from medical images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of brain tumor segmentation from T1-weighted MRI, and show that our approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art fully-supervised methods, while requiring significantly less labeling effort.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is currently the golden standard for thyroid nodule diagnosis. Ultrasound (US) images are commonly used to guide the FNAC procedure. In this paper, we present an automatic segmentation approach to assist the interpretation of US images of thyroid nodules. The approach consists of preprocessing, region proposal generation, segmentation refinement, and classification. In the preprocessing step, the image is denoised using non-local mean filtering and the specular reflection is removed via spherical harmonics. Region proposals are generated by an adapted variant of the selective search algorithm.

We address the problem of automatic lung tumor contour annotation from 4D computed tomography (CT) scans, i.e., stacks of 3D CT volumes acquired over the treatment period. Previously, we had developed a fully-automated algorithm based on a deformable model to track the tumor between volumes; however, it required 4 to 6 hours to run on a single patient. In this paper, we revisit this problem with the goal to achieve real-time performance, i.e., under 30 minutes per patient. Towards that end, we first identify the parts of the previous algorithm that accounted for the large run time. We then develop strategies to speed up those parts. In particular, we speed up the initialization of the deformable model by using an annotated reference scan; we speed up the deformation step by using a coarse-to-fine strategy that iteratively refines the contour; and we speed up the runtime by using all available volumes for the contour propagation, rather than just the two adjacent volumes.

We study the topology of surfaces for molecular Stark energy, alignment, and orientation generated by combined permanent and induced electric dipole interactions. The topology of surfaces provides a geometric framework to understand the behavior of these interactions. We find that the Stark energy surface is always homeomorphic to a sphere, but the alignment and orientation surfaces can have much more complex topologies. In particular, we identify a class of molecules for which the orientation surface has the topology of a torus. We also find that the alignment surface can have the topology of a sphere, a torus, or a Klein bottle, depending on the relative strengths of the permanent and induced dipole interactions.

 Our results provide a new way to understand the behavior of molecular Stark energy, alignment, and orientation based on the topology of the corresponding surfaces.

We consider solitons in a globally coupled hard-core bosonic system, which is described by the Gross-Pitaevskii type equations with the repulsive delta interaction and a two-body attractive/repulsive potential. There exist two different types of solitons in the system, the bright and dark solitons. By using the variational method, some new results on these solitons are obtained. It is shown that the attractive interaction always stabilizes the bright solitons, while the repulsive interaction always destabilizes the bright solitons. The effect of the two-body potential on the solitons is discussed. The dark solitons always exist in the system if the two-body potential is attractive enough, while they may disappear if the two-body potential is repulsive.

Efficient Smoothing of Dilated Convolutions for Image Segmentation. In this paper, we improve the efficiency of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image segmentation tasks. We observe that existing works either suffer from decreased performance due to the downsampling of multi-scale inputs or the increased computational cost for processing these inputs entirely, resulting in slow inference especially on architectures with many dilated convolutional layers. To address these issues, we propose an efficient smoothing method for dilated convolutions, which is designed to reduce the computational cost of processing inputs with many dilation layers while maintaining the performance. Our method works by adaptively adjusting the dilation rate of each layer based on the local structure of the input, allowing the network to concentrate on the most informative regions while suppressing the computational cost on less important areas. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on two public segmentation benchmarks, Cityscapes and CamVid, with state-of-the-art performance and improved efficiency.

Deep learning has recently become an important tool for the diagnosis and prognosis of various diseases. We present a novel deep learning framework for the automated segmentation and function prediction of biventricular cardiac masses. These masses result from either tumor growth or benign structural abnormalities and can be found in patients with primary cardiac tumors, metastases, or cardiomyopathies. Our framework utilizes a fully convolutional neural network architecture combined with a 3D attention module to segment the masses from magnetic resonance (MR) images. We then use the segmented masses to calculate a series of function metrics that have been shown to be predictive of adverse cardiac events. We evaluated our method on 100 MR images and compared the results to those obtained with a support vector machine (SVM) and a fully automated mass segmentation (AMS) method.

Automated segmentation of the mandible from CT scans is a prerequisite for various clinical applications such as computerized tomography (CT) radiotherapy, diagnosis, and surgery. However, this task is challenging due to the similarities in bone and soft tissue densities and the complications of anatomical variations. In this paper, we present a robust and fully automated method for segmenting the mandible from CT scans. Our method is based on a combination of hierarchical clustering and watershed segmentation. The hierarchical clustering is used to obtain a initial segmentation, which is then refined by the watershed segmentation. The proposed method was evaluated on 20 CT scans and the results show that our method is accurate and reliable.

Selection models with monotone weight functions in meta-analysis pose several interesting mathematical challenges, which become particularly acute when the selection process is sequential. We investigate selection models that can be described by a weighted average, where the weights are non-increasing functions of the selection probability. Such models occur in various applications, including systematic reviews in medicine, and have attractive theoretical features. We characterize the selection probabilities and the expected summary effect in both the fixed-effort and the random-effort models. In the fixed-effort model, we show that the selection probabilities converge to a limit distribution at the fastest possible rate, and that the expected summary effect is asymptotically normal. In the random-effort model, we derive the limiting distribution of the expected summary effect, showing that it is asymptotically normal under weak conditions on the effort distribution.

In this paper, we present a light-weight encoder-decoder based network, CFPNet-M, for real-time segmentation of multimodal biomedical images. CFPNet-M is designed to perform dynamic programming based pixel-wise labeling of images in multiple modalities via a shared encoder-decoder architecture. In our design, the encoder extracts the semantic content of the input multimodal biomedical images, while the decoder performs pixel-wise labeling in a bottom-up manner. To handle the variability in the input images, a confidence based fusion strategy is proposed at the decoder stage. Specifically, we employ a confidence score to measure the reliability of the features from different modalities, and use it to guide the fusion process. With the proposed approach, CFPNet-M enables effective refinement of the segmentation results, while maintaining real-time performance.

Abstract - Lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide, and computerized tomography (CT) is increasingly used for lung cancer screening. However, the current practice of manual analysis of CT images is tedious, time-consuming, and subjective. In this paper, we present a fully automated framework for lung tumour detection, segmentation and analysis, which is designed to assist radiologists in clinical practice. Our framework comprises a tumour detection module based on a deep learning architecture, a segmentation module based on a multi-atlas label fusion strategy, and an analysis module that evaluates the tumour volume, mean tumour diameter and tumour-free lung volume. To evaluate the performance of our framework, we conducted a retrospective study on 252 CT scans from 222 patients, and the results show that our framework can achieve an accuracy of 92.3%, a sensitivity of 91.5% and a specificity of 93.2% for lung tumour detection, and an accuracy of 91.5% for lung tumour segmentation.

 Furthermore, our framework can assist in clinical decision making, as it achieves an accuracy of 89.5% for tumour volume measurement, 86.9% for mean tumour diameter measurement, and 91.5% for tumour-free lung volume estimation.

We present a design for a scalable, compact, and cost-effective real-time quantum random number generator (QRNG) with robust entropy collection, hidden Markov model (HMM) postprocessing, and a simple user interface. Our design consists of off-the-shelf hardware components and open-source software. We discuss improvements made to the state-of-the-art HMM-based postprocessing technique to enhance robustness and discuss a simple technique to assess the entropy before postprocessing. Our design performs well in terms of power consumption, speed, and quality of the generated random numbers when compared to existing designs.

 Keywords: Quantum Random Number Generator (QRNG), Entropy Estimation, Hidden Markov Model (HMM), Random Number Generation, Real-time System

We present a simple, practical optimisation of the measurement of relativistic distortions in large-scale structure, focusing on the thermal and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ and kSZ) effects as observable in galaxy surveys. We optimise the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for a given survey, finding that the SNR is optimised by splitting the survey area into many independent patches, and stacking the signal from patches that are seen at high angle to the line-of-sight to the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This method - "stacking by angle" - reduces the noise from astrophysical contaminants and CMB anisotropies, while keeping the signal from the tSZ and kSZ effects coherent. In narrow redshift bins, stacking by angle optimises the SNR even in patches as small as ∼5° (∼10⁶ galaxies). However, in wide redshift bins where the survey is deeper, the SNR is optimised for patches with diameters of ∼30°-50° (∼10⁷-10⁸ galaxies). We provide a simple form of the optimal survey mask for stacking by angle, and show that the optimal mask does not depend on the optional galaxy clustering measurement.

We find that deep neural networks trained to solve partial differential equations can develop robust and generalizable solutions when trained in a hierarchical fashion. We present experiments on several models showing that this approach enables a fast and efficient computational paradigm to simulate high-dimensional fluid flows and solve the Laplace equation with minimal training data. In contrast to recent work on learned numerical methods that focus on discretizing PDEs, our approach views the neural network as a generalized function approximation and the solution as an implicit function of the input coordinates and the parameters of the PDE. We show that this approach is particularly beneficial for solving PDEs in high-dimensional domains where the manual design of an explicit discretization would be impractical.

 Our results show that DNNs are capable of solving PDEs in complex geometries, and that solutions predicted by DNNs are of high quality and generalize well to new inputs. In contrast to recent work on learned ODE solvers, we do not require any ad-hoc regularization methods and show that simple (and unstable) architectures are able to learn to solve PDEs.

In this paper, we present an efficient traversability analysis approach for autonomous terrain vehicles using stereo vision. In order to perform real-time analysis of the terrain, we employ a stereo-based approach, where the terrain surface is reconstructed from the stereo pair using semi-global matching (SGM). The reconstructed surface is then segmented into traversable and non-traversable regions using a normal-based segmentation algorithm. To further improve the accuracy of the segmentation, we then analyze the superpixel surface of the reconstructed 3D terrain. Finally, we employ a machine learning approach to train a classifier for the traversability analysis. The experimental results, conducted on different datasets, show that our proposed approach can achieve accurate and efficient traversability analysis for autonomous terrain vehicles.

In this paper, we propose a linear framework for image segmentation and inpainting that involves a curvature penalty. Our approach is based on the minimization of a functional that consists of an edge-stopping term, a region-size regularization term, and a curvature penalty term. The edge-stopping term ensures that the solution remains close to the initial image, the region-size regularization term encourages the solution to have a prescribed number of regions, and the curvature penalty term helps to preserve the curvature of the initial image. The resulting functional is minimized via a linear programming algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of image segmentation and inpainting problems, and show that our method produces results that are comparable to, or better than, state-of-the-art methods. 

 Our approach offers several advantages over existing methods for image segmentation and inpainting.

Recent works have shown that neural architecture search (NAS) is feasible for medical image segmentation. However, directly applying NAS to this problem can be very time-consuming, as the search space can easily reach millions of architectures. In this work, we present a coarse-to-fine NAS (C2FNAS) approach that significantly reduces the search space, while maintaining promising performance. Our approach consists of two stages: a coarse search that selects a subspace of architectures that are likely to generalize well, followed by a fine search that refines the architectures within the selected subspace. The subspace is selected such that architectures within it can use a shared backbone while still allowing customization via a lateral connection. We apply our approach to 3D medical image segmentation, and search for architectures that can utilize a shared 3D U-Net backbone for segmentation of multiple anatomical structures.

Recent advances in 4D MRI imaging have made it possible to longitudinally acquire whole-tumor MRI volumes as a 4D dataset, with each 4D-volume acquired over several minutes, for a given patient. However, due to the limitation of computational resources, it is challenging to utilize the 4D dataset for tumor growth prediction, which requires modeling the complex spatio-temporal correlations and the varying growth rates across different patients. In this paper, we propose a novel Spatio-Temporal Convolutional LSTM (STCL) model, which learns to predict tumor growth rates by utilizing both spatial and temporal information from the 4D longitudinal patient data. We introduce a spatio-temporal convolutional layer, which performs 3D convolution on each slice of the 4D volume, and a stack of LSTM layers that model the temporal dependencies at each spatial location. We optimize the entire STCL model using a stacked sparse-reward learning framework, which incorporates a sparse-reward structure to push the model towards learning the sparse representations of the highly varying growth rates. Finally, we evaluate our method on a large dataset of 4D MRI longitudinal volumes from glioblastoma patients, and show that our method achieves significant performance improvement over the state-of-the-art.

Image segmentation serves as a fundamental computer vision task with numerous applications in object recognition, image editing, and robotics. Although recent advances in deep learning have resulted in significant performance improvements in pixel-level image segmentation, directly predicting pixel-wise labels from images is challenging due to the infinite number of labels (i.e., pixels) in an image. Additionally, for many real-world applications, predicting a pixel-wise label map is not sufficient. Instead, more detailed and structured semantic descriptions of images, such as object bounding boxes, instance labels, or relationship annotations, are often needed. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in pixel-level image segmentation as well as more advanced segmentation settings, including instance-level segmentation, object detection, and relationship cosegmentation. We cover both bottom-up and top-down segmentation approaches, including methods based on deep learning, graph cuts, and conditional random fields.

Recent progress in deep learning enables numerous applications of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in medical image analysis, especially in image segmentation. However, most of the existing methods treat image segmentation as a binary-wise or pixel-wise classification problem and thus segment the objects in a constant scale, which may cause the loss of object boundary information or lead to uneven segmentation results for objects with different sizes. In this paper, we propose a 3D deep coarse-to-fine framework to achieve volumetric medical image segmentation, which can preserve the boundary information and handle objects with different sizes. Within our framework, we first utilize a 3D CNN to extract multi-scale features and then adopt a conditional random field (CRF) to refine the segmentation results on each scale. To effectively train the 3D CNN, we further propose a novel 3D adversarial example generation method, which can add diversity to the training samples and thus accelerate the training process. The proposed method has been evaluated on the ISBI challenge 2016 and 2017 segmentation datasets and compared with other state-of-the-art methods.

We propose a neural network approach for optimizing stochastic processes that can be expressed as constrained optimization problems with a large number of dimensions. The proposed method is motivated by optimal stopping problems, where the goal is to choose a stopping time for a given stochastic process that maximizes the expected cumulative rewards. We introduce a deep neural network that learns a ranking of the response surfaces over the decision space, without relying on the explicit form of the reward function. We show that the proposed approach can effectively optimize a wide class of reward functions, including possibly non-differentiable and non-convex functions. We demonstrate the performance of our method on a synthetic problem and two optimal stopping problems: maximizing the expected lifetime of a stochastic process and maximizing the expected cumulative rewards in a sequential classification problem. Our results show that the proposed method can effectively optimize these problems and improve the state-of-the-art.

We present a new evaluation criterion for cell membrane segmentation of atomic force microscopy (AFM) images based on human perception. We show that the widely used criterion measuring the difference between the ground truth and the predicted membrane mask has the drawback of being insensitive to certain types of errors that are readily noticeable to human observers. To address this problem, we propose a new evaluation criterion that is inspired by the observation that perception-based errors are more significant than geometric measures when evaluating segmentation quality. Specifically, we first extract a set of image features that are relevant to human perception of segmentation quality. We then adopt an attention mechanism that, given a segmentation mask, automatically computes the importance of each pixel by aggregating the features over a small support region around each pixel. The proposed criterion combines the attention weights and the geometric error between the predicted and ground truth masks.

Recent progresses in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in specialized image segmentation tasks, yet their usage remains limited to the domain they are trained on, lacking the ability to generalize to unseen domains. In this paper, we tackle the problem of segmenting medical images acquired from different domains (e.g., different institutions or different modalities) by designing a MixSearch framework that learns a universal segmentation architecture applicable to all domains. Given a set of domains with limited labeled samples each, our approach first utilizes domain-specific pre-trained models as fixed initialized prior models to build domain-adaptive segmentation architectures, and then a meta-learning based approach is introduced to refine these prior models into domain-generalized segmentation architectures. Specifically, we propose a novel progressive meta-learning framework, where a sequence of few-shot learners with increasing complexity are learned in an iterative manner. Each few-shot learner is first fine-tuned with domain-specific data to adapt to individual domains and then further trained on the mixed dataset to learn domain-generalization. We evaluate our method on segmenting lymph nodes from different institutions in the CAMELYON-train and -test datasets, as well as segmenting pulmonary nodules in CT images from two different institutions, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

In this article, we continue the study of symmetries of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) initiated in [AS2020]. The concept of symmetry is well-developed for linear ODEs, but much less so for nonlinear ones. The main goal of this article is to provide a partial answer to the following question: given a nonlinear ODE, how can one determine if it displays a symmetry, and if so, what is the form of that symmetry? As a case study, we consider the modified Emden equation, a classical model in astrophysics, geometry, and topology. This equation possesses an infinite-dimensional group of symmetries, generated by four independent basic symmetries. In this article, we determine all nonlinear differential equations that are symmetries of the modified Emden equation.

In this work, we develop a numerical method for radiative transfer in randomly textured slabs, which are uniformly coated with contaminant of known thickness and optical properties. The method utilizes the scattered light technique, where the coated rough surface is replaced by an effective perfect diffuser. This approach, when combined with the Monte Carlo method further enables us to model the radiative transfer in the contaminant layer and the substrate. We present a numerical example to demonstrate the application of the method to calculate the reflectance of a rough silicon wafer coated with SiO2 of known thickness and refractive index. We show that the coated rough surface exhibits higher reflectance than the bare substrate at near-normal incidence due to the multiple scattering in the rough surface and the additional reflections at the interface. However, the reflectance decreases with increasing angle of incidence, and at some angle, the bare silicon becomes more reflective than the coated rough silicon.

Reproducibility in data analysis is a growing concern in introductory statistics, as students are increasingly working with large datasets and complex models. R Markdown is a powerful tool for creating reproducible data analyses, but it is underutilized in introductory statistics. This paper describes a project that introduces R Markdown to undergraduate students in a statistical inquiry course. In groups, the students replicated a data analysis of a case study, first using only Excel and Word, then using R Markdown. The project was evaluated through interviews, surveys, and observations. The results suggest that R Markdown helped the students to be more precise in their reporting, use correct statistical methods, and work collaboratively.

Recent semi-supervised instance segmentation methods mostly focus on modeling spectral or spatial relationships between pixels in different images through consistency and/or similarity learning. These methods either treat all pixels within an object as a unit or assign labels independently at each pixel without considering their spatial coherence, which limits their ability to capture complex object structures. In this paper, we propose a Mask-guided Sample Selection (MSS) approach for training a semi-supervised pixel-level classifier. Given a pixel of interest, our method selects its class-consistent neighboring pixels as semantic contextual samples through a learned mask. We pose the learning of the mask as a binary classification problem, where the mask is the decision boundary between the foreground (object) and background (rest of the image). Specifically, given an initial guess of the mask, we minimize the cross-entropy loss by iteratively refining the mask through gradient descent.

We survey and assess recent advances in transfer learning for medical image segmentation with FCNs. The main focus is on semantic segmentation, but we also touch on instance segmentation. We first provide a comprehensive overview of the field from three different perspectives: 1) What are the existing datasets and evaluation metrics for medical image segmentation? 2) What are the state-of-the-art methods for medical image segmentation? 3) How do existing methods perform on a common benchmark?

We present a stable multiscale Petrov-Galerkin finite element method for high frequency acoustic scattering computation. The method is based on the proper generalized decomposition (PGD) framework, where the scattering problem is decomposed into a coarse problem and a set of fine problems. The coarse problem is solved using the standard finite element method, while the fine problems are solved using a spectral element method. The multiscale error estimator is derived using the concept of the generalized eigenvalue problem. The proposed method is evaluated on several numerical examples, including the scattering of a plane wave by a cylinder and the scattering of a Gaussian beam by a sphere. The results show that the method is accurate and efficient for high frequency scattering computation.

Arxiv is a website where researchers can upload their work and make it available to other researchers. "Coherent averaging" is a technique used in quantum mechanics and other fields to calculate the expected value of a variable over a set of possible outcomes, given some probability distribution. The expected value is a measure of the average value of a variable over a set of outcomes, and it can be used to predict the behavior of a system. The coherent averaging method can be used to calculate the expected value of a variable in a system that is described by a set of linear equations. The method can be used to find the solution to a set of linear equations, given some initial conditions and a set of probabilities for the outcomes of the variables in the system.
